headings.text: 🌳 Decision tree: which shape should this interface have?

notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time

The section answers one question, which shape should this interface have?, and the answer is almost never decided on speed. The options differ in contract enforcement, cacheability, browser reach, failure mode and operational weight, and the last one is what you live with.

Concept map

The sync-or-async fork comes first because it decides the failure mode before any protocol is named; everything else is a branch of it, and the choice framework joins the branches back up.

Green is CORE, blue is SUPPORTING; 91–93 holds one CORE note (gRPC) and two SUPPORTING ones, 101–103 three SUPPORTING. Neighbours: HTTP semantics below this section, realtime transports beside it.

The full option-by-attribute matrix and the which-shape decision tree the choice framework

Decision tree: which shape should this interface have?

The binding question is whether the caller waits; the default leaf on the synchronous side is plain REST, and every other leaf has to earn its extra machinery. The choice framework owns this tree and its full matrix; it is drawn here until that note is migrated.

  • Queue or event (queues, webhooks): changes if the user is on the other end waiting for a result on screen; then it's a job with a status.
  • 202 + job (long-running jobs): changes if partial output is the product, as with tokens; then stream it.
  • SSE or WebSocket (choosing a realtime transport): changes if updates are rare; a poll is simpler.
  • REST (REST): changes if one screen needs many resources over a slow link and parallel fetches aren't enough.
  • gRPC (gRPC): changes if a browser must call it directly; then it needs gRPC-Web and a proxy, or REST at the edge.
  • GraphQL (GraphQL): changes if the clients are few and their shapes stable; compound REST views are cheaper to operate.

At a glance

  • The one big idea: pick the interface by who waits and who consumes, not by speed; then pick the controls (precondition, idempotency key, deadline, DLQ) that bound its failure mode.
  • The two most-confused pairs: REST vs RPC over HTTP (POST /getUser is RPC, and loses caching and safe retry); a queue vs a log (one consumer and delete, or many groups at their own offsets).
  • Ten minutes before a tech discussion: this decision tree; the conditional read-and-write sequence in REST; the round-trip derivation in the same note; the matrix in the choice framework; the gRPC-behind-L4 picture in gRPC in production.

notes.title: REST — Resources, Verbs, Statelessness, HATEOAS
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics · Fielding 2000, ch. 5: Representational State Transfer · 📜 RFC 8288: Web Linking · MDN: HTTP request methods · OpenAPI Specification

TL;DR

REST is a style, not a protocol: the URL names a thing, the method says what happens to it, and every request carries everything needed to answer it. That is what lets every cache, proxy and retrying client in the middle act correctly without reading your docs. The price is round trips: one per resource, so a screen made of many resources is slow on a slow link.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:GET /orders/8f2cache: fresh? serve itany instance answers (no session)200 + ETag "v7"later If-None-Match "v7"304, no bodywrite with If-Match "v7"200 + "v8", or 412 if someone wrote first

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does "stateless" forbid? Session state on the server between requests. Resource state in the database is fine.
Which REST constraint do real APIs skip? HATEOAS: responses carrying the links to what you can do next.
Who in the middle relies on the uniform interface? Caches, proxies, gateways and retrying clients: they read the method, not your docs.
Round trips for 1 order + 10 line items, strictly? 11 serial; 2 if the children are fetched in parallel.
An action with no noun, like a transfer? Make it a resource: POST /transfers → 202 + Location, with an id to retry against.
Draw by hand: a conditional read, then a conditional write Client → cache → API: 200 + ETag, If-None-Match → 304, If-Match → 200 or 412.

The idea

A mobile app loads an order, edits it and saves. With an API that ignores HTTP's meaning, the save is POST /updateOrder: when the response is lost the client can't tell whether to retry, and the CDN caches nothing because everything is a POST. Meanwhile a support agent saves the same order from a laptop, and the last write silently wins.

REST changes three things on the same flow. The order is a resource with a URL, so a GET is something any cache may reuse and any instance may answer. The save is PUT /orders/8f2 with If-Match: "v7", so the method says it is idempotent and the precondition says which version it replaces: the second writer gets 412 instead of overwriting. And the action that has no noun, a refund, becomes POST /refunds, a resource with an id and a status, so it has something to retry against.

The trade: HTTP's whole middle (caches, proxies, conditional requests, retries) works on your API for free, and you pay a round trip per resource.

How it works

A read through a shared cache, then two writes racing for the same version. The response headers, not the client, decide what the middle may do.

The two conditional headers do opposite jobs: If-None-Match saves bytes on a read, If-Match stops a lost update on a write.

Constraint What it lets the middle do
Stateless Any instance serves any request, so the load balancer needs no stickiness and a crashed or redeployed instance loses nothing.
Uniform interface A cache knows GET is safe and may be reused; a client or proxy knows PUT and DELETE may be retried. Method properties are owned by safe, idempotent, cacheable.
Cacheable The response declares its own reuse with Cache-Control and ETag; nothing is cached unless the server says so. Directives in HTTP caching.
Layered The client can't tell the origin from a CDN, gateway or WAF, so you insert one without touching clients.
Hypermedia (HATEOAS) Typed links (Link: <…>; rel="next", RFC 8288) let a client follow the API instead of building URLs. Usually skipped.

The weakness is arithmetic, and it is the whole case for GraphQL and compound endpoints:

screen = 1 order + n line items          ← one request per resource
serial = (1 + n) · RTT = 11 · 120 ms ≈ 1.3 s   ← n = 10 on a 120 ms cellular link
parallel items = 2 · RTT ≈ 240 ms        ← the fix is fewer serial hops, not a faster server

Evolution

Lineage:1997 HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068)2000 Fielding names REST (dissertation, ch. 5)2017 OpenAPI 3.02022 RFC 9110 consolidates HTTP semantics2026 RFC 10008 adds QUERY
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): the default style for public and partner APIs, described by OpenAPI (3.2.1, Sep 2026).
  • Changed in RFC 10008 (Jun 2026): QUERY is a safe, idempotent, cacheable method that carries a body, so a complex search no longer has to choose between a huge query string and an uncacheable POST /search. Servers, proxies and caches need support before you rely on it; OpenAPI 3.2 can describe it.
  • What's next: QUERY support spreading through proxies and frameworks. What won't change: the middle can only help with what the method and headers tell it.

On the wire

Captured on 16 Oct 2026 from a 25-line http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15, curl 8.7.1), headers trimmed to the ones that matter:

GET /orders/8f2                                  # ① first read
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
ETag: "v7"                                       # the version a later request can name
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, must-revalidate   # per-user: revalidate every time, but cheaply
{"id": "8f2", "status": "packed", "v": 7}

GET /orders/8f2   If-None-Match: "v7"            # ② "I have v7"
HTTP/1.0 304 Not Modified                        # headers only, no body

PUT /orders/8f2   If-Match: "v7"   {"status":"shipped"}       # ③ replace v7
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
ETag: "v8"

PUT /orders/8f2   If-Match: "v7"   {"status":"cancelled"}     # ④ a second writer, still on v7
HTTP/1.0 412 Precondition Failed                 # lost update refused, not applied

Break it: statelessness is a property of where state lives, not of HTTP. Two instances behind a round-robin balancer:

from itertools import cycle
class Instance:                                   # one app server behind a round-robin LB
    def __init__(self): self.sessions = {}
    def login(self, user): self.sessions["s1"] = user; return "s1"
    def me_session(self, sid): return self.sessions.get(sid, "401 who are you?")
    def me_token(self, token): return token.split(":")[1]   # stand-in for verifying a signed token
lb = cycle([Instance(), Instance()])
sid = next(lb).login("asha")                       # request 1 lands on instance A
print("session:", next(lb).me_session(sid))        # request 2 lands on instance B
print("token:  ", next(lb).me_token("signed:asha"))
# look for: the session lookup fails on the second instance, the token works on any instance
# naive belief predicts: both print asha, because "the server knows who I am"

Run on Python 3.15: session: 401 who are you?, token: asha. The session needs sticky routing; the self-contained request works anywhere, which is what scaling out and invisible deploys depend on.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i twice with If-None-Match shows 304 and no body on the second read; If-Match with a stale ETag shows 412, and the resource is unchanged.
  • In production: 304 share and CDN hit ratio per route (near zero on a read-heavy API means validators are missing); per-screen latency and requests per screen from the client, against per-request p99 on the server.
  • Bounded by: a lost update or a double-applied write → If-Match preconditions on every replace, an idempotency key on every POST that creates (idempotency keys), and actions modelled as resources with ids.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: REST is an architectural style: resources with URLs, HTTP methods with fixed meanings, self-contained requests, and responses that declare their own cacheability. The payoff is that caches, proxies, conditional requests and retries all work on your API for free. What almost nobody ships is HATEOAS. So most "REST APIs" are HTTP APIs with good resource modelling, and the honest weakness is round trips: one per resource.

Q · Mechanism — What does statelessness buy you, and what does it cost? Every request carries its credentials and context, and the server keeps no session between requests. So any instance can answer any request: the balancer needs no stickiness, scaling out is adding instances, and a deploy or crash loses nothing (the Break it shows the failure when that's not true). The cost is repetition: a token on every request, and a multi-step flow that must become a resource with its own id, such as a draft, instead of a server-side conversation.

Q · Trade-off — Where does resource modelling stop fitting, and what do you do? It fits CRUD and fights actions: "send this email", "retry this job", "transfer between accounts". If the action has a lifecycle (it can queue, fail, be retried or inspected later), make it a resource, POST /transfers returning 202 and a Location; that gives you an id, a status and something to retry against (long-running jobs). If it is a synchronous computation with no lifecycle, an RPC-shaped endpoint is honest (RPC-style APIs). Contorting it into PUT /accounts/1/balance is worse than either.

Q · Failure — The app feels slow, but server p99 and CPU look fine. What's happening? The resource model is costing round trips: a screen needing an order and ten line items makes eleven serial calls, about 1.3 s on a 120 ms link, while each call is fast. You'd confirm it with requests per screen and the client waterfall, not server metrics. Fixes in order: parallelise the children, add an include or compound view endpoint for that screen, and only then consider GraphQL. Check 304 share too: validators turn repeat reads into header-only responses.

Q · Design — Design a public REST API that three partners will depend on for years. A public contract can't be un-shipped, so design how it changes first: additive-only, a written definition of breaking, Deprecation and Sunset headers (versioning and deprecation). The contract is OpenAPI, generated from or checked against the code; one error envelope, cursor pagination and idempotency keys on creates (REST API design). Watch per-consumer error and schema-validation rates first: an aggregate hides one partner breaking.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Idempotent methods the safe ones + PUT, DELETE POST is not; PATCH only by design spec: RFC 9110 §9.2.2
Cacheable by default GET, HEAD POST only with explicit freshness; QUERY is cacheable with the body in the key spec: RFC 9110 §9.2.3, RFC 10008
Lost-update guard If-Match → 412 the optimistic-concurrency primitive spec: RFC 9110 §13.1.1
Screen of 1 + 10 resources ≈ 1.3 s serial, ≈ 240 ms parallel 120 ms RTT, server time ignored derived

Pitfalls

  • "Stateless means the server can't store anything"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "stateless" sounds like "no state", and session-free servers feel like they forget everything.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the database is full of state, and that's the point. What's forbidden is the server remembering this client's conversation outside an addressable resource, like a wizard half done in memory.
    ↳ Think instead: no session state; resource state is fine. A multi-step flow becomes a resource with an id.
  • "Choosing REST means I get HTTP caching" (a belief I held)
    ↳ Why it's tempting: cacheability is the advantage every comparison table gives REST over gRPC and GraphQL.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: you get the ability. Frameworks commonly send no validator, or no-store, and everything behind Authorization is per-user, so nothing is reused until you set ETag and Cache-Control on purpose.
    ↳ Think instead: caching is opt-in per route. Split public resources from per-user ones, and add validators so repeat reads become 304s.
  • Not the same: If-None-Match vs If-Match
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both take an ETag and both are "conditional requests".
    ↳ Difference: If-None-Match on a read says "send it only if it changed" and answers 304. If-Match on a write says "apply only if it hasn't changed" and answers 412.
    ↳ Think instead: None-Match saves bytes; Match prevents lost updates. Idempotency keys stop duplicate writes, not overwrites.
  • "It isn't REST without HATEOAS, so nothing is REST"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's literally true of Fielding's definition, and it wins arguments.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's useless in a design discussion. The other constraints still pay for themselves, and HATEOAS pays off only for generic clients that discover the API at run time, not hand-written ones.
    ↳ Think instead: say which constraints you keep and why; use typed links where they help, as with rel="next" pagination.
  • Don't call POST /getUser REST.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's HTTP and JSON, and "REST API" is the default label.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every call is a POST, so caches reuse nothing, clients and proxies can't retry safely, and the team expects REST's benefits that the design threw away.
    ↳ Do instead: model nouns where they exist; where the domain is truly verbs, choose RPC on purpose and name it.
  • Don't force a strict resource model on a chatty screen.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one resource per endpoint is clean, and purity feels like quality.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a screen built from eleven resources costs eleven round trips, about 1.3 s on a 120 ms link, while every server metric looks healthy.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler fix first: parallel fetches, then an include parameter or one view endpoint for that screen, before reaching for GraphQL.
  • Shelf life: the constraints and the round-trip arithmetic are durable. QUERY support in proxies, frameworks and OpenAPI tooling is what will move.

Connections

Path:method propertiesRESTREST API designthe choice framework
  • Builds on HTTP methods (PUT vs PATCH lives there) and headers: REST adds a style, not new mechanics.
  • Owned elsewhere: HTTP caching owns the Cache-Control directives; choosing the right code owns 202, 409, 412, 422.
  • Contrasts with gRPC (internal, schema first) and GraphQL (round trips first).
  • Bounded by idempotency keys: what makes a retried create safe.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: where sync request/response is chosen for a service boundary.
  • Composes with schemas and contracts: OpenAPI is how a REST contract is enforced.

notes.title: REST API Design — Naming, Pagination, Filtering, Versioning, Error Envelopes
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs · 📜 RFC 8288: Web Linking · 📜 RFC 9110 §12.5, §15.5: content negotiation, client errors · OpenAPI Specification

TL;DR

Five choices decide whether an API is still pleasant in year three: plural nouns with opaque ids, opaque cursors instead of offsets, an allow-listed filter grammar, the version in the URL, and one application/problem+json error shape everywhere. Each is cheap at design time and a breaking change later. The cursor matters most: offsets are wrong on a changing list, not just slow.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:GET /v1/orders?limit=25server reads limit + 1 rows by (created_at, id)200 + Link: <…cursor=…>; rel="next"client echoes the cursor untouchedseek after that row ─no nextdone
GET /v1/orders?sort=emailnot on the allow-list400 + application/problem+json with type and the allowed fields

Recall

Prompt Answer
Offset pagination's bug, beyond speed? Inserts and deletes shift the window: rows silently repeat or vanish between pages.
What must a cursor key on? A unique, totally ordered tuple, such as (created_at, id), encoded opaquely.
Which error field do clients branch on? type, a stable URI. title and detail are for humans (RFC 9457 §3.1).
Who in the middle sees a URL version but not a header one? Caches (key on URL), access logs, WAF and gateway path rules, dashboards.
How does a page say "there's more" without COUNT(*)? Fetch limit + 1; the extra row's existence emits rel="next".
Draw by hand: an export where rows arrive between pages Client → API → DB: page 1 + cursor, insert at top, page 2 seeks after cursor, no repeats.

The idea

A partner syncs 40,000 orders into their warehouse with ?page=2&per_page=25. Between page 1 and page 2, two new orders land at the top of the sort. Page 2 is "rows 26–50" of a list that just grew by two, so it starts with two orders the partner already has. Nothing errors. With deletes, rows are skipped and the warehouse is quietly short.

A cursor anchors the next page to a row, not a position: "everything after (10:07, o7)". Inserts above the anchor don't move it, so page 2 is exactly the rows after the last one seen. The cursor is base64 and undocumented on purpose, so you can change what's inside it (add a shard, change the tie-breaker) without breaking the clients that stored it.

The trade: you give up "jump to page 12" and a cheap total count, and in return pages stay correct and constant-cost on a list that never stops changing.

How it works

The same export with a cursor. The insert lands between the two page requests, and page 2 still starts after the last row the client saw.

The client only echoes the cursor, so the server stays free to change it.

Decision What actually happens
Names and ids Plural nouns (/orders/o7), actions as resources (REST). Opaque ids: sequential integers leak volume and invite enumeration, and can't be changed later.
Pagination Opaque cursor over a unique sort tuple; limit capped server-side; rel="next" (RFC 8288 §2.1.1) ends when absent. No total count by default.
Filtering and sorting Query parameters with one documented grammar (?status=shipped&sort=-created_at); fields outside the allow-list get 400 naming the allowed set.
Versioning Major version in the path (/v1/). A header version needs Vary: Accept on every cacheable response, or the cache serves v1 to a v2 client.
Errors application/problem+json: type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extension members (RFC 9457 §3.2) such as a correlation id and a field-error list.

The offset cost is arithmetic, and it's the smaller argument:

offset page p, size s → the DB produces p·s + s rows, returns s   ← OFFSET is skipped, not seeked
page 400, size 25     → 10,000 rows read for 25 returned            ← grows with depth
cursor page           → one index seek + s + 1 rows                 ← same cost at any depth

Evolution

Lineage:2000 Fielding names REST2016 RFC 7807 problem details2017 RFC 8288 web linking2023 RFC 9457 obsoletes 78072025 RFC 9745 Deprecation header
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): cursor pagination and a single error envelope are standard in public APIs; OpenAPI describes all five choices.
  • Changed in RFC 9457 (Jul 2023): a registry of common problem type URIs (§4.2), guidance on how to treat multiple problems (§3), and on type URIs that can't be dereferenced (Appendix D). The media type is unchanged, so a 7807 producer still parses.
  • What's next: QUERY (RFC 10008) gives complex searches a cacheable body instead of a huge query string. What won't change: offsets stay wrong on a moving list.

On the wire

Captured on 22 Nov 2026 from a 25-line http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15.0, curl 8.7.1), Server and Date trimmed:

GET /v1/orders?limit=3
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Link: </v1/orders?limit=3&cursor=WyIyMDI2LTExLTIyVDEwOjA3OjAwWiIsICJvNyJd>; rel="next"
{"data": ["o9", "o8", "o7"]}           # cursor decodes to ["2026-11-22T10:07:00Z", "o7"]: the last row's sort tuple

GET /v1/orders?limit=3&cursor=WyIy…Jd    # echoed, never built by the client
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Link: </v1/orders?limit=3&cursor=WyIy…NCJd>; rel="next"
{"data": ["o6", "o5", "o4"]}

GET /v1/orders?sort=customer_email      # not on the allow-list
HTTP/1.0 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/problem+json
{"type": "https://api.example.test/errors/invalid-sort", "title": "Unsupported sort field",
 "status": 400, "detail": "customer_email is not sortable.", "allowed": ["created_at", "updated_at"]}

The 400 with the allow-list is an availability control: no index, no sort, no full scan.

Break it: offset vs cursor on a list that grows between pages, in SQLite.

import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:"); db.execute("create table o(id integer primary key, ts integer)")
db.executemany("insert into o values(?,?)", [(i, 100 + i // 2) for i in range(1, 11)])
off = lambda n: [r[0] for r in db.execute("select id from o order by ts desc, id desc limit 3 offset ?", (3 * n,))]
p1 = off(0); last = db.execute("select ts, id from o where id = ?", (p1[-1],)).fetchone()
db.executemany("insert into o values(?,?)", [(11, 200), (12, 201)])            # 2 rows land on top
cur = [r[0] for r in db.execute("select id from o where (ts, id) < (?, ?) order by ts desc, id desc limit 3", last)]
print("p1", p1, "offset p2", off(1), "cursor p2", cur)
# look for: offset page 2 repeats rows already on page 1; cursor page 2 doesn't
# naive belief predicts: offset is only slower, so both page 2s match

Run on Python 3.15.0, SQLite 3.54.1: p1 [10, 9, 8] offset p2 [9, 8, 7] cursor p2 [7, 6, 5]. Two rows repeat with no error. A cursor on ts alone also broke: a tie at the page boundary skipped row 8.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i a list endpoint: a Link … rel="next" header and an opaque cursor; a disallowed sort returns 400 with Content-Type: application/problem+json.
  • In production: per request, p99 by query shape (sort × filter set), not by endpoint; per consumer, error rate by problem type; page-depth distribution; cursor-decode failures (a client building cursors).
  • Bounded by: one client's heavy query starving the shared DB pool → allow-listed fields, a hard limit cap, a statement timeout, a separate pool or replica for exports, and per-consumer rate limits.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Five decisions: plural nouns with opaque ids; opaque cursors over a unique sort key, because offsets duplicate or skip rows when the list changes; an allow-listed filter grammar, because every filterable field is an index promise; the version in the URL, because caches, logs and gateways see it; and one RFC 9457 error envelope with a stable type, so clients write one handler. All five are cheap now and breaking later.

Q · Mechanism — Why is a cursor correct where an offset isn't? An offset names a position in a list that changes underneath the client: insert two rows at the top and page 2 starts two rows earlier, so it repeats them; delete and it skips. A cursor names the last row seen, by a unique tuple such as (created_at, id), and the next page is "rows after it", an index seek that inserts above don't move. The tuple must be unique: on the timestamp alone, two rows sharing a millisecond at a page boundary get skipped, which the Break it reproduced.

Q · Trade-off — URL versioning or header versioning? Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.x.v2+json) is purer: the URL stays canonical. URL versioning wins on operations: the version is visible in access logs, CDN cache keys, WAF rules and support tickets, curl-able, and routable with a path rule; a header version needs Vary: Accept everywhere, or a cache mixes versions. Use the path for breaking versions and content negotiation for genuine representation variants. Either matters less than an additive-only policy (versioning and deprecation).

Q · Failure — A partner adds ?filter= on an unindexed column across 200 million rows. What happens? The query becomes a full scan that holds a database connection for its whole run. Repeated across a partner's sync job, the scans exhaust the connection pool, and every endpoint sharing that pool fails while CPU looks idle. You'd confirm it with pool wait time and p99 by query shape. Fix: the controls in Bounded by, starting with a statement timeout so a bad plan fails in a second.

Q · Design — Design the error contract for an API twenty teams integrate against. The binding constraint is that clients branch on errors in code. So type is a stable URI per error class and part of the contract; title and detail can be reworded or localised freely; status mirrors the HTTP code (choosing the right code owns which one). Extension members carry a correlation id that traces share and every field error, not just the first. Watch error rate by type per consumer first: one team can be fully broken inside a flat aggregate. Gateway placement is in service communication patterns.

Compare

Decision Option A Option B When you'd pick it
Pagination offset / limit opaque cursor Offset only for small, stable lists a person pages through by number; cursor for everything else, always for sync and export.
Versioning path /v1/ Accept media type Path for breaking versions of a public API; media type for representation variants.
Total count always opt-in or estimate Opt-in: on a large filtered table the count is the most expensive part of the request.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Error media type application/problem+json RFC 9457 (Jul 2023) obsoletes RFC 7807 spec: RFC 9457
Default problem type about:blank when no type is given; title then matches the status phrase spec: RFC 9457 §4.2.1
Malformed vs semantically wrong 400 vs 422 Unprocessable Content 422: syntax correct, instructions not processable spec: RFC 9110 §15.5.1, §15.5.21
Offset page 400, size 25 10,000 rows produced, 25 returned cursor page: one seek + 26 rows derived

Pitfalls

  • "Offset pagination is fine, just slower at depth"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every comparison leads with OFFSET performance, and on a static test fixture the pages look right.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: on a live list, inserts shift the window and rows repeat; deletes make rows vanish. The Break it repeated two rows with no error, which in an export is silent data loss.
    ↳ Think instead: offsets are a correctness bug on a changing list; lead with that, then the cost.
  • "A timestamp is a good enough cursor"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: created_at is already the sort key and looks unique at a glance.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: two rows in the same millisecond at a page boundary: ts < ? skips one, ts <= ? repeats one. It appears only under concurrent writes, so tests pass.
    ↳ Think instead: key on a unique tuple, (created_at, id), compared as a row value, not as two ANDed conditions.
  • Not the same: 400 vs 422
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean "your request is wrong", and many frameworks return 400 for everything.
    ↳ Difference: 400 is malformed (unparseable JSON, bad framing); 422 is well-formed but semantically invalid (source and destination accounts are the same).
    ↳ Think instead: can the server parse it? No → 400; yes but it can't act on it → 422. Neither is ever retried.
  • Don't build a filter grammar for three known queries.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a generic ?filter= feels future-proof and saves writing endpoints.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every column combination becomes a possible query plan, and the unindexed ones become full scans that drain the shared connection pool.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: three named endpoints, or a grammar limited to an allow-list of indexed fields.
  • Don't put secrets or PII in query parameters.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: filters already live there, and ?email=… is the obvious lookup.
    ↳ What goes wrong: URLs are written to access logs, proxy and CDN logs and browser history, so the value ends up in systems with far wider access than your database.
    ↳ Do instead: look up by opaque id, or send sensitive filters in a body (POST /orders/search, or QUERY where supported).
  • Shelf life: the five decisions are durable. Problem-type registries and QUERY support in gateways and SDKs are what will move.

Connections

Path:RESTREST API designRPC-style APIsschemas and contracts
  • Builds on REST: the constraints these five decisions implement.
  • Owned elsewhere: choosing the right code owns which status; idempotency keys owns safe creates.
  • Composes with schemas and contracts: OpenAPI publishes the allow-lists and problem types; CI catches breaking changes.
  • Bounded by rate limiting: per-consumer limits keep one sync job from owning the pool.
  • Used by versioning and deprecation: the policy around the path version chosen here.
  • Drilled in keyset pagination: the query plan behind the cursor.

notes.title: RPC-Style APIs & When They Beat REST
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §9.2, §9.3.3: method properties, POST · gRPC over HTTP/2: idempotency and retries · JSON-RPC 2.0 Specification

TL;DR

RPC exposes procedures (POST /v1/CalculatePrice) instead of resources, so nearly every call is a POST. You keep TLS, auth, status codes and tracing, and you give up exactly two things: the middle can't cache it, and nobody may retry it automatically. Worth it when the operation is a verb with no lifecycle, or when both ends are yours and a typed schema matters more than a CDN.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:POST /v1/CalculatePriceCDN: a POST, so forwardgateway routes by pathhandler runs the procedure200 + resultclient may retry only if the method is declared idempotent or carries a key

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two things you lose when every call is POST? Shared caching and method-implied idempotency, so no automatic retries.
Can a cached POST response answer a later POST? No. It can only serve a later GET or HEAD (RFC 9110 §9.3.3).
The test for "procedure or resource"? Would anyone ask later "what happened to it?" If yes, it needs an id: a resource.

The idea

A pricing service exposes POST /pricing-calculations because "REST means nouns". Nobody ever fetches a calculation again; there's no id worth storing, no state, no lifecycle. The noun is fiction, and the team pays for it in naming meetings and in clients confused about whether GET /pricing-calculations/{id} exists.

RPC names the operation honestly: POST /v1/CalculatePrice with a typed request and response. What changes on the wire is the method. A shared cache won't reuse the response, and RFC 9110 §9.2.2 says a proxy must not retry it, so the retry property you'd have had from PUT has to be declared per method instead. gRPC is this style with a schema: every call is an HTTP/2 POST, and calls aren't assumed idempotent unless marked.

The rule that sorts the cases: a transfer, an import or a refund is phrased as a verb but fails the test, because "did it work?" must outlive the request. Those are resources (REST owns that move). A price quote, a validation or a ranking passes.

The trade: an honest shape for verb-heavy domains, paid for with the CDN and with retry safety you now have to write down per method.

How it works

The same lookup exposed both ways through one shared cache. Only the GET lets the middle help.

The verdict is capacity arithmetic once the operation is a read that repeats:

origin requests, REST read  = n · (1 − h)      ← h = cache hit ratio
origin requests, RPC POST   = n                ← a cached POST never answers a POST
h = 0.9 → RPC sends 10× the origin load        ← same function, different method
Rule What actually happens
One path per method POST /v1/CalculatePrice, not POST /api with an action field: the gateway, rate limiter, access log and metrics all key on the path.
Retry safety is declared Mark idempotent methods in the schema, or require an idempotency key; gRPC retries only calls marked idempotent or proven not started.
What the middle does A CDN forwards every POST; a proxy won't retry one (RFC 9110 §9.2.2); a gateway can still authenticate, rate-limit and route by path.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): typed RPC (gRPC) is the common internal style; JSON-RPC 2.0 (2010, updated 2013) carries MCP and editor protocols.
  • What's next: QUERY (RFC 10008, Jun 2026) gives read-shaped calls a safe, cacheable method with a body, which removes one reason to use POST for a lookup. What won't change: a POST gets no cache and no automatic retry.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i the same lookup as GET and as POST through a CDN: the GET repeats with an Age or cache-hit header; the POST never does.
  • In production: per route, CDN hit ratio and origin requests per second; per method, the duplicate-effect rate (repeated idempotency keys, double charges) after client timeouts.
  • Bounded by: a retried POST applying twice → an idempotency key per side-effecting method, and retries only on methods the schema marks idempotent.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: RPC models the API as procedures rather than resources, so over HTTP it's mostly POST to a method-named path. You keep status codes, auth, TLS and tracing; you lose shared caching and method-implied idempotency. It beats REST when the domain is verbs with no lifecycle, such as pricing, scoring or validation, and when both ends are internal and a schema with codegen matters more than a CDN. That last case is gRPC.

Q · Mechanism — What exactly do you give up when everything is a POST? Two things. Caching: RFC 9110 lets a POST response be stored only with explicit freshness and a matching Content-Location, and even then it can serve only a later GET or HEAD, never another POST, so a CDN in front of RPC is a pass-through. Retries: PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, so clients and proxies may resend them; a POST carries no such promise, and a proxy must not retry it. You put the property back per method, with an idempotency key or a schema annotation.

Q · Trade-off — When does RPC genuinely beat REST, and when does it lose? It wins when the operation is a computation nobody looks up again (a quote, a fraud score, a ranking) and resource-modelling it would invent a noun with no lifecycle. It wins internally, where nothing passes through a CDN and a typed contract with generated clients beats cacheability: that's gRPC. It loses for public read-heavy APIs, where the hit ratio is origin capacity, and for anything with a lifecycle, where the caller will need an id, and adding one later breaks the contract.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Cached POST answering a POST never may serve a later GET or HEAD only spec: RFC 9110 §9.3.3
Proxy auto-retry of POST must not non-idempotent methods spec: RFC 9110 §9.2.2
gRPC call method HTTP/2 POST not assumed idempotent unless marked spec: gRPC PROTOCOL-HTTP2
Origin load at 90 % hit ratio 10× for RPC n vs n·(1−h) derived

Pitfalls

  • "RPC is the old way; REST replaced it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: SOAP and CORBA were RPC, and REST arrived as the reaction to them.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: gRPC is RPC and is the common internal style today; JSON-RPC carries MCP and editor protocols. What faded was untyped, undisciplined RPC, not the style.
    ↳ Think instead: RPC with a schema and declared retry rules is a sound choice; RPC as POST /api {"action": …} is not.
  • Not the same: a verb-shaped name vs a procedure
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: "transfer funds" and "calculate price" both read as actions.
    ↳ Difference: a transfer can queue, fail, be retried or audited, so it needs an id and a status; a price quote is computed and forgotten.
    ↳ Think instead: ask "what happened to it?" If anyone will, model a resource (POST /transfers → 202); if not, a procedure is honest.
  • Don't assume a POST RPC is safe to retry.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the client library retries on timeout, and most handlers "probably" don't double-apply.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the response was lost, not the request, so the retry charges twice; nothing in HTTP told the client that was unsafe.
    ↳ Do instead: mark idempotent methods in the schema and require an idempotency key on the rest.
  • Don't reach for RPC on a public read-heavy API.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one POST per operation is quick to build and looks uniform.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the CDN reuses nothing, so at a 90 % hit ratio the origin takes ten times the load, and conditional 304s disappear.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: plain GET on a resource for reads, and keep procedures for the verbs.
  • Shelf life: the two losses are fixed by RFC 9110. QUERY support in CDNs and frameworks is what will shift the read-shaped cases.

Connections

Path:REST API designRPC-style APIsgRPCthe choice framework
  • Builds on safe, idempotent, cacheable: the two properties RPC forfeits.
  • Contrasts with REST: pick it when the operation has a lifecycle or a CDN is in the path.
  • Used by gRPC: the same style with a schema, codegen and deadlines.
  • Bounded by idempotency keys: how a retried POST stays single-effect.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: where internal call style is chosen.

notes.title: gRPC — Protocol Buffers, Codegen, Status Codes, the Four Call Types
notes.html:
References

📜 gRPC over HTTP/2 (PROTOCOL-HTTP2) · grpc.io: Core concepts and RPC life cycle · gRPC status codes · protobuf.dev: Encoding · Envoy router filter: x-envoy-retry-grpc-on

TL;DR

You write the contract once in a .proto, generate a typed client and server in every language, and a call becomes POST /package.Service/Method on an HTTP/2 stream with a protobuf body. The wire carries field numbers, not names, and the outcome is one of 17 status codes, which is what retrying clients and proxies act on. You buy a schema, streaming and deadlines; you pay in browser reach, curl-ability and a middle that must speak HTTP/2.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:.protogenerate stubsstub.Get(req, timeout=2s)POST /orders.v1.Orders/Get + grpc-timeout: 2S5-byte prefix + protobufhandlergrpc-status: 0 in trailerstyped reply, or RpcError(UNAVAILABLE)

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four call types? Unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming.
What names a field on the wire? Its number: key = (field_number << 3) | wire_type. Names never travel.
An unknown method returns which HTTP status? 200, with grpc-status: 12 (UNIMPLEMENTED).
Which status code is the retryable one? UNAVAILABLE (14); DEADLINE_EXCEEDED may hide a completed write.
Who in the middle acts on it? An L7 proxy or mesh: routes on :path, retries on grpc-status in headers.
Draw by hand: one call through a proxy, with a retry Stub → proxy → server: POST /Svc/Method, UNAVAILABLE → proxy retries → OK.

The idea

A Python checkout service calls a Go pricing service with hand-written JSON over HTTP. The pricing team renames total to total_minor and ships. Every response is still 200, the Python side reads total as missing, defaults it to 0, and orders go out free. Nothing failed, so nothing alerted. Meanwhile a slow pricing call hangs for 30 s, because each client picked its own socket timeout.

gRPC changes both on the same call. The contract is a .proto in a shared repo, and both sides compile against generated code, so the rename breaks a build instead of production. On the wire the field is number 2, so even an old binary still reads the value correctly. The call carries a deadline the server can see, and its outcome is a typed status the caller's library turns into an exception, not a 200 with an empty body.

The trade: a compiled contract, typed failures and first-class streaming, paid for with a codegen pipeline, a binary wire you can't read with curl, and a path that must speak HTTP/2 end to end.

How it works

A unary call through a mesh proxy. The proxy can route and retry without knowing your schema, because the method is in :path and the outcome is a status code.

The proxy retried because the failure came as a status in the response headers. A status in trailers, after a body, is past the point where a retry is safe.

Rule What actually happens
IDL and codegen service and message blocks in a .proto; protoc or buf generate writes stubs per language. The .proto is the contract; its evolution rules live in schemas and contracts.
Wire mapping One call is one HTTP/2 stream, each message has a 5-byte prefix, and status arrives in trailers: owned by gRPC on HTTP/2.
Status codes 17 codes, 0–16, in grpc-status. The code tells the caller what to do next: retry (UNAVAILABLE), fix the request (INVALID_ARGUMENT), or stop (FAILED_PRECONDITION).
Deadlines The client sets one, the wire carries the remaining time as grpc-timeout, and the server sees it. Propagation and budgets: gRPC in production.
The middle An L7 proxy or mesh routes per call on :path and retries on grpc-status. An L4 balancer sees one TCP connection and pins every call to one pod.

Protobuf is why the wire is small and why names are free to change. The value is a varint, low 7 bits per byte:

08 96 01               ← protobuf.dev's example: field 1 = 150
08 = 1 << 3 | 0        ← field number 1, wire type 0 (varint)
96 01 = 0x16 + 0x01·128 = 150   ← little-endian groups of 7 bits
0a 03 38 66 32         ← captured below: field 1, type 2 (length-delimited), 3 bytes "8f2"
10 f4 03 = field 2, varint 500  ← total_minor; 8 bytes for the whole Order

Evolution

Lineage:2008 protobuf open-sourced (Jul)2015 gRPC open-sourced2016 gRPC 1.0 (Aug)2018 gRPC-Web GA (Oct)2024 protobuf Editions (release 27.0, May)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the default typed RPC between services; meshes and Envoy treat it as first-class.
  • Changed in protobuf Editions: edition = "2023" replaces syntax = "proto2"/"proto3" with per-feature settings, such as field presence. The wire format didn't change, so old and new binaries interoperate.
  • What's next: browser reach still goes through gRPC-Web (unary and server streaming only, as of Nov 2026). What won't change: numbers on the wire, a status per call, HTTP/2 underneath.

On the wire

The contract, then one call to it. Captured on 22 Nov 2026 from a grpcio 1.85.3 server (Python 3.13.14) on 127.0.0.1, called with curl 8.7.1 over h2c, headers trimmed:

service Orders { rpc Get(GetRequest) returns (Order); }      // unary
message Order  { string id = 1; int64 total_minor = 2; }    // numbers are the wire contract

POST /orders.v1.Orders/Get HTTP/2        # path = /package.Service/Method
content-type: application/grpc           # servers SHOULD answer 415 to anything else
te: trailers                             # lets the server spot a proxy that drops trailers
grpc-timeout: 2S                         # remaining time, not a clock time; server saw 1.998 s
<00 00000005> 0a 03 38 66 32             # prefix (not compressed, 5 bytes), then GetRequest{id:"8f2"}

HTTP/2 200
content-type: application/grpc
<00 00000008> 0a 03 38 66 32 10 f4 03    # Order{id:"8f2", total_minor:500}
grpc-status: 0                           # in trailers: the real result

Break it: a call to a method the server doesn't have, with the same server and req.bin holding the request above.

curl -sv --http2-prior-knowledge -H 'content-type: application/grpc' -H 'te: trailers' \
  --data-binary @req.bin http://127.0.0.1:50551/orders.v1.Orders/Delete -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep '^< '
# look for: HTTP/2 200 with grpc-status 12 in the response headers block, and no body
# naive belief predicts: HTTP/2 404, because the path doesn't exist

Run on 22 Nov 2026: HTTP/2 200, grpc-status: 12, grpc-message: Method not found!, sent as a single headers block (trailers-only). An access log that keys on HTTP status records this failure as a success.

Measure it

  • See it: grpcurl -v or curl --http2-prior-knowledge -v show :path, grpc-timeout and grpc-status; correct is 200 plus grpc-status: 0 on success.
  • In production: per method, a grpc-status histogram (rising 14 means dependency trouble, rising 4 means budgets); per backend, calls per second, whose skew means connection pinning.
  • Bounded by: a hung call → a deadline on every call; a retry storm → retries only on UNAVAILABLE with a capped attempt count and the deadline spanning all attempts.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: gRPC is typed RPC over HTTP/2. The .proto defines services and messages, codegen gives every language a stub, and each call is a POST to /package.Service/Method on its own stream, with a protobuf body and a status code at the end. It gives four call types for the same machinery, deadlines the server can see, and a contract that breaks builds rather than production. It costs browser reach and a gRPC-aware middle.

Q · Mechanism — What does gRPC add on top of HTTP/2, given that it is HTTP/2? Nothing at the transport: a call is an ordinary stream with a POST, a path naming the method, and length-prefixed messages (gRPC on HTTP/2). What it adds is above: an IDL with generated clients, four defined call shapes, a deadline carried as grpc-timeout, 17 status codes with agreed retry meaning, and interceptors as the hook for auth, tracing and metrics. Envoy, for example, retries on unavailable only when the status arrives in response headers, never in trailers.

Q · Trade-off — gRPC or REST for a new internal service? Choose on contract and consumers, not speed. gRPC wins when several teams or languages share an interface, when calls stream, or when a deep fan-out needs deadlines and cancellation. REST wins when a browser, partner or curl-wielding operator is the consumer, or when HTTP caching matters, because gRPC calls are POSTs and no shared cache reuses them. One team, one language, one consumer: either works, and the schema usually tips it toward gRPC once the second consumer appears.

Q · Failure — Error dashboards are green, but a client team reports failures. What's going on? The dashboards count HTTP status, and every gRPC failure travels inside a 200 (the Break it). The resource running out is visibility: real failures sit in grpc-status. Confirm it with grpcurl -v against one method, or by comparing the proxy's per-method grpc-status stats with its HTTP response-code stats. Fix: alert on grpc-status per method, split 14 (retryable) from 4 (budget) and 13 (bug), and make the access log record the gRPC code.

Q · Design — Design the service surface twelve teams in four languages will call. The binding constraint is that the .proto is shared while deploys are independent, so the design is a compatibility policy: one schema repo, buf breaking in CI (schemas and contracts), versioned packages (orders.v1), stubs published per language. Calls run through a mesh that balances per call, with a deadline set at the edge and propagated (gRPC in production). The edge speaks REST or gRPC-Web to browsers. The first signal to watch is DEADLINE_EXCEEDED by originating service. Placement follows service communication patterns.

Compare

Call type Client sends Server sends Watch out for When you'd pick it
Unary 1 message 1 message nothing special ordinary request and response
Server streaming 1 many a slow reader stalls the stream (flow control) feeds, log tails, model tokens
Client streaming many 1 the deadline covers the whole upload bulk upload, telemetry batches
Bidirectional many many ordering holds within the call only; you own the protocol inside live sync between services

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Call types 4 unary, server, client, bidi streaming spec: grpc.io core concepts
Status codes 17 (0–16) OK 0, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED 4, UNIMPLEMENTED 12, UNAVAILABLE 14 spec: gRPC statuscodes.md
Message prefix 5 bytes 1 flag + 4-byte big-endian length spec: PROTOCOL-HTTP2
grpc-timeout value ≤ 8 digits + unit H M S m u n spec: PROTOCOL-HTTP2
Field key (number << 3) | type 1 byte for fields 1–15 spec: protobuf.dev encoding
Example Order 8 bytes id "8f2" + total_minor 500 measured: grpcio 1.85.3, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "We use gRPC because it's faster than REST"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: binary payloads and multiplexing sound fast, and benchmarks show smaller messages.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: for most services the time goes to the database and downstream calls, not to JSON parsing. Lead with speed and the next question is a benchmark you didn't run.
    ↳ Think instead: the case is the contract, streaming and deadlines; payload size matters only at high message rates.
  • Not the same: renaming a field vs renumbering it
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both look like "changing the field" in a diff.
    ↳ Difference: the binary wire carries only the number, so a rename is invisible there and breaks only code and JSON. A new number is a different field, so old readers lose the value.
    ↳ Think instead: numbers are permanent, names are cosmetic on the binary wire; schemas and contracts has the full rules.
  • "A failed RPC shows up as a 5xx"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every HTTP API you've monitored worked that way.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the HTTP status reports the transport. The call's outcome is grpc-status, so UNIMPLEMENTED, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED and INTERNAL all arrive inside a 200.
    ↳ Think instead: monitor grpc-status per method, never HTTP codes, for gRPC traffic.
  • Don't retry on every non-OK status.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a generic "retry on error" wrapper is one line.
    ↳ What goes wrong: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED may come back after the write has happened, and INVALID_ARGUMENT fails identically every time, so retries duplicate writes or burn load.
    ↳ Do instead: retry UNAVAILABLE only, with capped attempts inside the deadline, plus an idempotency key on writes.
  • Don't expose gRPC to browsers or partners when REST would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one protocol everywhere feels consistent.
    ↳ What goes wrong: browsers need gRPC-Web and a translating proxy, with no client or bidi streaming; partners expect curl, OpenAPI and caching.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: REST or gRPC-Web at the edge, gRPC behind it.
  • Shelf life: the wire format, status codes and call types are stable. gRPC-Web's streaming limits and protobuf editions are what move.

Connections

Path:RPC-style APIsgRPCgRPC in productionschemas and contracts
  • Builds on HTTP/2 framing: streams give one call per stream and many calls per connection.
  • Owned elsewhere: gRPC on HTTP/2 owns trailers and the 5-byte prefix; gRPC load balancing owns the L4 problem.
  • Bounded by gRPC in production: deadlines, budgets and connection age.
  • Contrasts with REST: browsers, partners and HTTP caching.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: where a service boundary picks sync RPC.

notes.title: gRPC in Production — Deadlines, Connection Age, Retries, Browsers
notes.html:
References

grpc.io: Deadlines · gRFC A9: Server-side connection management · gRFC A6: Client retries · grpc.io: Load balancing

TL;DR

Three things decide whether gRPC behaves in production. Calls ride one long-lived connection, so balancing has to happen per call (an L7 proxy, client-side balancing, or at least a capped connection age). A deadline is a budget to divide down the chain, and handlers must check it. Retries need a policy, because gRPC ships none.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:edge sets deadline 2 seach hop forwards the remaining timehandler checks is_active()retry only UNAVAILABLE, inside the deadline
server sets MAX_CONNECTION_AGEGOAWAY max_age (±10% jitter)client reconnectsL4 balancer places it on a new pod

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why does an L4 balancer pin gRPC? It picks a backend per TCP connection; every call shares that one connection.
MAX_CONNECTION_AGE default? Infinite. The server must set it, plus a grace period.
Does the server's work stop at the deadline? Only if the handler checks the context; propagation doesn't kill your loop.

The idea

A gateway calls an orders service on ten pods behind a Kubernetes Service, which balances at L4. The gateway's one channel carries every call on one connection, so one pod runs hot while nine idle, adding pods changes nothing, and the balancer's metrics look healthy. In the same chain every hop sets its own 2 s timeout, so when the edge gives up, inner hops keep working for nobody.

The trade: per-call balancing and budgeted deadlines cost a proxy hop or client logic, plus handler discipline; without them, scaling out and timeouts quietly stop working.

How it works

The same client, two data paths; red is the hot pod.

Behind L4, connection age is the only lever: a permanent pin becomes a bounded one.

Rule What actually happens
Connection age At MAX_CONNECTION_AGE (±10% jitter) the server sends GOAWAY with max_age, lets calls finish for _GRACE, and the client reconnects through the balancer.
Per-call balancing An L7 proxy or mesh parses HTTP/2 and spreads streams; client-side balancing picks per call itself (trade-off below).
Deadline on the wire The deadline is a point in time, but gRPC sends the remaining duration, so clock skew between hosts doesn't matter. Java and Go propagate it to outgoing calls by default; C++ needs it enabled.
Retries Retries are on, but there's no default policy. A service-config retryPolicy names codes (usually UNAVAILABLE) and maxAttempts, and the deadline spans all attempts.

The budget is divided, not repeated:

edge deadline = 2,000 ms              ← set once, at the edge
A's own work ≈ 200 ms → B gets ≤ 1,800 ms   ← A forwards what's left, not a fresh 2 s
B calls C with 1,200 ms               ← B keeps 600 ms for its own work and a fallback
same 2 s at every hop → A fails first, C keeps working   ← wasted capacity, no error at C

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): connection age, deadlines and retry policy are long-standing gRFCs in every major language.
  • What won't change: a long-lived multiplexed connection needs a per-call decision somewhere; proxyless xDS only moves where it's made.

On the wire

Three grpcio 1.85.3 servers (Python 3.13.14) behind a round-robin TCP proxy on 127.0.0.1; one channel makes 60 calls, 100 ms apart. Run on 22 Nov 2026:

opts = [("grpc.max_connection_age_ms", 1000),        # GOAWAY after ~1 s (±10% jitter)
        ("grpc.max_connection_age_grace_ms", 500)]   # let in-flight calls finish
server = grpc.server(futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(4), options=opts)
# default (no opts):   TCP connections=1  calls per backend=[60, 0, 0]
# age 1,000 ms:        TCP connections=6  calls per backend=[21, 21, 18]

Nothing failed in either run: the pin shows only in per-backend counts.

Break it: a handler of ten 100 ms steps, called with a 250 ms deadline, with and without a ctx.is_active() check.

for step in range(10):
    time.sleep(0.1)                                   # stand-in for a query or a downstream call
    if checks and not ctx.is_active(): return b""     # the only thing that stops the work
# look for: the unchecked handler still runs all 10 steps after the client got DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
# naive belief predicts: both handlers stop at 250 ms, because "gRPC cancels the call"

Run on 22 Nov 2026: both clients got DEADLINE_EXCEEDED; the checking handler stopped after step 2, and the other ran all ten steps, about 1 s, for nobody.

Measure it

  • See it: per-backend call counts after scaling out (even means balanced); remaining deadline at handler entry, per hop, shrinking and never starting fresh.
  • In production: per pod, calls per second and CPU skew; per method, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED by originating service; per connection, age.
  • Bounded by: a pinned pod → MAX_CONNECTION_AGE with grace, or L7 balancing; abandoned work → a propagated deadline plus handlers that check it; retry storms → maxAttempts and retry throttling.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: gRPC fails quietly in two ways. Behind L4, a client's calls share one connection, so one pod gets everything: balance per call, or at least cap connection age. And a deadline is a budget divided down the chain, which handlers must check to stop work. Add a retry policy too, since gRPC ships none.

Q · Mechanism — How does a deadline travel, and why doesn't clock skew break it? The client holds an absolute deadline, but the request carries grpc-timeout with the time left, such as 1800m. The server converts it back to its own clock, so skew never enters, and an onward call sends what's left after its own work. In the capture in gRPC, the server saw 1.998 s of 2 s. The timeout hierarchy owns the general inequality.

Q · Trade-off — Client-side balancing or a proxy? A proxy or mesh sidecar keeps policy in one place you change without redeploying clients, in every language, and adds retries, mTLS and telemetry; you pay a hop on every call. Client-side balancing removes the hop, but every language needs discovery and health logic. Default to the mesh; earn client-side balancing on latency-critical paths with few languages. Plain L4 is never the answer.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Connection-age jitter ±10% spreads reconnect storms spec: gRFC A9
60 calls, one channel, L4 60 / 0 / 0 three backends, round-robin per connection measured: grpcio 1.85.3, 22 Nov 2026
Same, age 1,000 ms 21 / 21 / 18 6 connections in ~6 s measured: grpcio 1.85.3, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Kubernetes balances my gRPC traffic"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a Service balances HTTP/1.1 traffic fine, and gRPC is "just HTTP".
    ↳ Why it's wrong: kube-proxy picks a backend per connection, and a gRPC client keeps one connection for all its calls: 60 of 60 in the run above.
    ↳ Think instead: balance per call: a mesh or L7 proxy, client-side balancing, or at least a capped connection age.
  • Not the same: a timeout vs a deadline
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "give up after N seconds" in client code.
    ↳ Difference: a timeout is local and starts fresh at every hop. A deadline belongs to the request, and each hop inherits what's left.
    ↳ Think instead: set one deadline at the edge and divide it, as in the derivation above.
  • "gRPC-Web gives the browser full gRPC"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it shares the .proto, the stubs and the name.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: browsers don't expose HTTP/2 frames or trailers, so gRPC-Web puts trailers in the body, needs a translating proxy such as Envoy, and supports unary and server streaming only (as of Nov 2026).
    ↳ Think instead: a browser gets a subset through a proxy; client and bidi streaming need a WebSocket or a server-side hop.
  • Don't jump to a mesh to fix one hot pod.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the mesh is the "proper" fix and solves balancing for good.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a control plane and sidecars, to fix one server setting.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler first step: MAX_CONNECTION_AGE with a grace period, then measure per-pod skew.
  • Shelf life: pinning and deadline arithmetic are durable; defaults and gRPC-Web's limits move.

Connections

Path:gRPCgRPC in productionschemas and contracts
  • Builds on gRPC on HTTP/2: why one connection carries every call.
  • Owned elsewhere: gRPC load balancing owns the balancer mechanics; the timeout hierarchy owns budget nesting.
  • Composes with service mesh: the usual home of per-call balancing and retry policy.
  • Bounded by timeouts, retries, backoff: jitter and retry budgets.

notes.title: GraphQL — One Endpoint, Client-Shaped Queries, N+1, Persisted Queries, Caching
notes.html:
References

📜 GraphQL Specification, September 2026 · 📜 GraphQL over HTTP (working draft) · graphql.org: Performance · graphql.org: Caching

TL;DR

One endpoint fronts a typed schema, and the client names exactly the fields a screen needs, so many REST round trips become one. The price is structural: a POST with a per-client body gives a shared cache nothing to key on, and the client now composes the query's cost.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:POST /graphql + queryparse and validate against the schemacost and depth check4xxresolvers run per fieldloader batches the keysdata (maybe partial) + errors

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why can't a CDN cache it by default? Every operation is POST /graphql; the meaning is in a body that varies per client.
N+1, precisely? A list resolver returns n items, then a child resolver fetches once per item: 1 + n queries.
What do persisted queries buy? A known set of documents sent by hash: bounded cost, short requests, GET-able.

The idea

A mobile home screen needs a user, their last five orders and each order's customer. Over REST that is a chain of calls, about one round trip per resource (REST owns the arithmetic). In GraphQL it is one request naming exactly those fields.

Then the server runs it: the orders resolver returns 50 rows and the customer resolver fires once per row, 51 database queries from one request. A loader that batches keys per tick makes it 2. And the CDN saw a POST, so it cached nothing.

The trade: one round trip per screen and a schema clients can introspect, paid for with lost HTTP caching, query-cost control that becomes your job, and one URL that tells your dashboards nothing.

How it works

One query through the edge and the server; the loader is what keeps resolver fan-out from reaching the database.

Rule What actually happens
Resolvers run per field Fan-out is by construction, not a bug: nested lists multiply (50 orders × 50 items × 20 reviews = 50,000 leaves).
Loader batching Keys are collected per request and per tick, then fetched once. Its cache is per request; shared across users it leaks data.
Cost control is pre-execution Depth limit, a complexity score weighting list sizes, a per-client budget: the point is to reject before paying.
The middle The CDN or gateway sees one URL and one method, so it can't cache or rate-limit per operation unless it parses the body or the client sends GET with a persisted-query hash.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026). The September 2026 edition (12 Nov 2026) starts an annual cadence; its changes are small (directives on directives, stricter @oneOf).
  • Changed in the GraphQL-over-HTTP working draft: queries may use GET, mutations over GET get 405, and with application/graphql-response+json a partial result is 294, so status codes mean something again.
  • What's next: that draft becoming a release. What won't change: the client shapes the query, so the server owns its cost.

On the wire

Captured on 22 Nov 2026 from a 25-line http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15, curl 8.7.1), following the draft's status rules:

POST /graphql   Accept: application/graphql-response+json
{"query": "{ order(id: \"8f2\") { id recs { sku } } }"}
HTTP/1.0 294                                         # partial success: data present, errors too
Content-Type: application/graphql-response+json      # tells the client the body is authoritative
{"data": {"order": {"id": "8f2", "recs": null}}, "errors": [{"message": "recs timed out", "path": ["order", "recs"]}]}

GET /graphql?query=mutation { cancel(id:"8f2") { id } }
HTTP/1.0 405 Method Not Allowed                      # GET is safe, so it must not mutate
Allow: POST

Break it: a model of the customer resolver, with and without a loader:

calls = []
def fetch(ids): calls.append(ids); return {i: f"cust-{i}" for i in ids}   # one DB query
orders = [{"id": n, "cust": n % 7} for n in range(50)]   # the list itself: 1 query
naive = [fetch([o["cust"]])[o["cust"]] for o in orders]   # customer resolver runs per order
print("naive  :", 1 + len(calls), "queries"); calls.clear()
keys = {o["cust"] for o in orders}                        # loader: collect this tick's keys
got = fetch(sorted(keys)); batched = [got[o["cust"]] for o in orders]
print("batched:", 1 + len(calls), "queries for", len(keys), "distinct customers", naive == batched)
# look for: query count for one request
# naive belief predicts: one query, because the client sent one request

Run on Python 3.15: 51 queries naive, 2 batched. One client request is not one unit of server work.

Measure it

  • See it: log queries per request with the loader off and on; correct is one query per resolver level, not per item.
  • In production: latency and error rate per operation name, not per endpoint; errors counted from the body or the 294 share; resolver p99 per field; rejected-by-cost count per client.
  • Bounded by: a query that fans out to thousands of resolvers → depth and complexity limits checked before execution, per-client budgets, and persisted queries only for untrusted callers.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: GraphQL puts one endpoint in front of a typed graph, and the client asks for exactly the fields it needs, so a screen is one round trip with no over-fetching. The costs are structural: HTTP caching goes, because everything is a POST, and the client controls query cost, so depth limits, cost analysis and persisted queries are requirements.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through N+1 and how a loader fixes it. Resolvers run per field and independently, so fifty orders mean fifty customer queries plus the list: 51 where one IN (…) would do. A loader defers: each resolver registers a key, and at the end of the tick the loader issues one batched fetch and hands results back, caching within the request so a repeated customer loads once. That cache must be per request, or one user's data reaches another.

Q · Trade-off — GraphQL or REST for a web app and two mobile apps? GraphQL's best case: three clients want different slices of one graph on different release cycles, where REST means over-fetching or an endpoint per client. You pay three ways: caching moves into your service, cost control is yours, and metrics must go per operation. Choose GraphQL when client diversity is real and first-party; stay on REST for a public, read-heavy, cacheable API. (The choice framework.)

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Queries, 50 orders + customer 51 naive, 2 batched 7 distinct customers measured: Python 3.15 model, 22 Nov 2026
Partial success 294 with application/graphql-response+json unregistered, so old clients treat it as 200 spec: GraphQL over HTTP draft §6.1
Mutation over GET 405 GET must stay safe spec: GraphQL over HTTP draft

Pitfalls

  • "GraphQL is faster than REST"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one round trip instead of several is a visible win on mobile.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it saves client round trips, not server work. Resolution and batching add work per request, and losing CDN offload can raise total cost on read-heavy traffic.
    ↳ Think instead: fewer round trips for the client, more work and less caching for you.
  • Not the same: 200 vs success
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: classic GraphQL servers answer 200 with an errors array, and dashboards count non-2xx.
    ↳ Difference: partial data plus errors is a degraded answer; a dashboard reading status codes calls it success.
    ↳ Think instead: count errors from the body or from 294, per operation name, from day one.
  • Don't expose arbitrary queries to untrusted callers.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: introspection plus free-form queries is GraphQL's selling point.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a stranger can send a nested query that fans out to tens of thousands of resolver calls before any limit trips.
    ↳ Do instead: persisted queries (trusted documents) for public clients, with depth and cost limits behind them.
  • Don't use GraphQL between services.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one graph for everything sounds consistent.
    ↳ What goes wrong: internal callers gain nothing from field selection and lose deadlines and a compiled contract.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler fit, gRPC or plain REST, for service-to-service calls.
  • Shelf life: resolvers, N+1 and the caching gap are durable. The GraphQL-over-HTTP status rules are a draft and may still change.

Connections

Path:gRPC in productionGraphQLwebhooks
  • Builds on REST: the round-trip cost GraphQL exists to remove.
  • Owned elsewhere: HTTP caching owns what a GET with Cache-Control lets the middle do.
  • Contrasts with gRPC: schema-first too, but server-shaped and for internal callers.
  • Composes with API authentication: authorisation moves to the field, not the endpoint.
  • Decided in the choice framework: where client diversity does and doesn't justify it.

notes.title: Webhooks — Signature Verification, Retries, Idempotency, Replay Protection
notes.html:
References

📜 Standard Webhooks spec 1.0.0 · 📜 RFC 2104: HMAC · Stripe: receive webhook events · GitHub: validating webhook deliveries

TL;DR

A webhook is your server making a POST into infrastructure you don't run, so their downtime becomes your retry queue. The receiver checks an HMAC over the id, a timestamp and the raw body, rejects old timestamps, and dedupes on the id, because delivery is at least once and a captured request can be replayed.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:eventsender signs id.timestamp.bodyPOST to the partnerverify signature, timestamp within 5 minseen this id? 2xx, skipenqueue, 2xx fastretry with backoff over daysdisable after giving up

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why must the timestamp be inside the signature? Otherwise a captured request verifies forever; the window bounds replay.
Why verify against the raw body? Re-serialised JSON changes bytes; the HMAC covers bytes, not your parsed object.
Who in the middle acts on a webhook? The receiver's firewall, LB and timeout; the sender's egress proxy against SSRF.

The idea

You send invoice.paid; their deploy returns 500 after committing, you retry, and they credit the invoice twice. A month later someone who logged one request replays it, and with an HMAC over the body alone it still verifies.

Three fields close those holes, and the Standard Webhooks spec names them: webhook-id (stable across retries, so the receiver can dedupe), webhook-timestamp (inside the signed string, so an old request fails the tolerance check), and webhook-signature, an HMAC-SHA256 over id.timestamp.body (idempotency keys owns the dedupe pattern). GitHub's X-Hub-Signature-256 covers the body only, so replay protection there rests on deduping X-GitHub-Delivery.

The trade: push is immediate and cheap per event, and you pay with a retry queue per receiver, signatures and an SSRF-safe egress path, because the receiver's failures are now yours to absorb.

How it works

One event, one failed attempt, one retry. Each attempt gets a fresh timestamp and signature but the same id.

Answering before the work keeps a slow handler from becoming a retry storm.

Rule What actually happens
Success Only a 2xx. 410 means disable the endpoint; 429, 502, 504 mean throttle; honour Retry-After.
Retries The spec's example schedule runs about three days with exponential backoff and jitter; Stripe retries live-mode events for up to three days. GitHub doesn't redeliver automatically.
Timeouts The spec recommends 15–30 s; GitHub records a failure after 10 s. Acknowledge fast, process from your own queue.
The middle The receiver's firewall may need static source IPs; the sender's egress should pass through a proxy that blocks private ranges, because the URL is customer-supplied.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): HMAC over a timestamped body is the common scheme across Stripe, GitHub and the Standard Webhooks spec.
  • Changed in the current Standard Webhooks text (read Nov 2026): asymmetric v2a signatures (ed25519) replace the deprecated v1a, so one key pair, held in a KMS, serves every endpoint; v1 HMAC stays.
  • What's next and what won't change: RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures (Feb 2024) is the standards-track alternative to bespoke headers. Retries, dedupe and the replay window stay the receiver's job.

On the wire

Break it: a Standard Webhooks v1 receiver on 127.0.0.1, sent four deliveries (Python 3.15, run 22 Nov 2026). The last route verifies after json.loads and json.dumps, as a framework that hands you parsed JSON would:

def sign(mid, ts, body):                  # base64(HMAC-SHA256(secret, "id.timestamp.body"))
    return "v1," + b64(hmac.new(SECRET, f"{mid}.{ts}.".encode() + body, sha256).digest())
ok   = hmac.compare_digest(sign(mid, ts, body), headers["webhook-signature"])  # constant time
code = 401 if not ok else 400 if abs(time.time() - ts) > 300 else 200 if mid in seen else 204
send("/raw",    "msg_1", now)             # → 204, processed
send("/raw",    "msg_1", now + 5)         # → 200, a retry: acknowledged, not reprocessed
send("/raw",    "msg_2", now - 600)       # → 400, valid signature, outside the 5-minute window
send("/parsed", "msg_3", now)             # → 401, re-encoded body: '"type":"invoice.paid",  "id"' lost a space
# look for: the replay and the re-encoded body both fail; the retry is acknowledged once
# naive belief predicts: a valid HMAC is enough, and parsed JSON verifies the same

All four results came back as commented: the signature proves who, the timestamp bounds when, the id stops a second credit.

Measure it

  • See it: the sender's delivery log (Stripe's Event deliveries tab, GitHub's Recent Deliveries) shows status, attempt count and the next retry per delivery; correct is one 2xx per event id.
  • In production: per receiver, delivery success rate, attempts per event, oldest undelivered event age; on the receiving side, signature failures and duplicate-id rate.
  • Bounded by: one dead partner starving everyone → a delivery queue per receiver with a retry budget and disable-after-days; replay → the timestamp window plus id dedupe; SSRF → an egress proxy blocking private addresses.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A webhook is you calling into someone else's infrastructure, so assume it's down, slow or behind a firewall. The sender retries with backoff and jitter for days, per receiver, and signs id.timestamp.body with HMAC. The receiver verifies against the raw bytes in constant time, rejects timestamps outside a few minutes, dedupes on the id, and answers 2xx before doing the work. Offer a cursor endpoint for catch-up.

Q · Mechanism — Design the signature. What exactly gets signed, and why each part? The message id, a Unix timestamp and the raw body, joined with dots, under HMAC-SHA256 with a per-endpoint secret. The timestamp makes replay expire; the id lets retries be deduped and stops an attacker swapping ids. Raw bytes matter because a re-encoded body no longer matches, which the Break it shows as a 401. Compare in constant time so timing doesn't leak the digest.

Q · Trade-off — Push webhooks or let partners pull an events feed? Push is immediate, but their downtime fills your retry queue and they must expose an endpoint. Pull moves both burdens to them: they fetch since a cursor, at their own rate, with no inbound port, which is the only option behind a corporate firewall. The mature answer is both from one per-receiver log: push from it with retries, and expose it as a cursor-paginated feed so a partner who missed a week catches up without a support ticket.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Example retry span ≈ 75.6 h over 10 attempts 5 s, 5 min, 30 min, then hours spec: Standard Webhooks 1.0.0
Stripe tolerance, retries 5 min; up to 3 days live mode, exponential backoff default (as of Nov 2026): Stripe docs

Pitfalls

  • "The HMAC proves the request is fresh"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a valid signature feels like a valid request.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it proves who produced the bytes, not when. Without a signed timestamp and a tolerance check, a logged request verifies forever; the 10-minute-old one in the Break it is refused only by the window.
    ↳ Think instead: signature for authenticity, timestamp for freshness, id for duplicates. All three, every time.
  • Not the same: replay protection vs idempotency
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both stop "the same request twice".
    ↳ Difference: replay protection rejects an attacker's resend after the window; idempotency makes the sender's legitimate retry, inside the window, harmless.
    ↳ Think instead: the window stops strangers, the id stops your partner's retries.
  • Don't do the work before answering.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: processing inline is simpler than a queue, and it works in testing.
    ↳ What goes wrong: under load the handler passes the sender's timeout (10 s on GitHub), the sender retries, and the retries add more load.
    ↳ Do instead: verify, dedupe, enqueue, return 2xx, and process from your own queue.
  • Don't fetch a customer-supplied URL from inside your network.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's just an outbound POST from a worker.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the URL field becomes a scanner for internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.
    ↳ Do instead: send through an egress proxy that refuses private and link-local addresses, from a subnet with no internal access.
  • Shelf life: the HMAC scheme and retry discipline are durable; vendor tolerances, retry spans and asymmetric signatures are what will move.

Connections

Path:GraphQLwebhooksqueues and event streamslong-running jobs
  • Builds on sync vs async: webhooks are the async push to systems you don't run.
  • Bounded by timeouts, retries, backoff: the jittered schedule the sender runs.
  • Owned elsewhere: API authentication lists HMAC beside the other mechanisms; idempotency keys owns dedupe.
  • Used by long-running jobs: the callback option for job completion.

notes.title: Message Queues & Event Streams — SQS/RabbitMQ vs Kafka, Delivery Semantics, Ordering, DLQs
notes.html:
References

Apache Kafka 4.4: Design, message delivery semantics · Amazon SQS: visibility timeout · Amazon SQS: dead-letter queues · AWS Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

TL;DR

A queue hides a message while one consumer works on it and deletes it on ack; a log keeps every message and lets each consumer group read at its own offset. Both deliver at least once and order only within a partition or message group, so every consumer is idempotent and nobody gets global order.
