Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:producer sendsbroker storesconsumer receives (queue: hidden for the visibility timeout · log: offset advances)processesack or commitDLQ

Recall

Prompt Answer
What makes a queue redeliver? No delete before the visibility timeout ends: 30 s by default on SQS.
Where does ordering hold? Per partition (Kafka) or per message group (SQS FIFO). Never across the topic.
Who in the middle decides redelivery? The broker: visibility timer on a queue, the committed offset on a log.

The idea

A worker takes 40 s per job and the visibility timeout is 30 s. At second 30 the broker shows the message again, a second worker takes it, and every job runs twice; on a payment queue that is a double charge.

The two shapes behave differently on purpose. A queue tracks each message: hide on receive, delete on ack, move to a dead-letter queue after maxReceiveCount failed receives. A log tracks only offsets: messages are retained for a period (Kafka's default log.retention.hours is 168), each consumer group commits its own position, and a new group can start from the beginning.

The trade: a queue gives per-message retry and a DLQ but no replay; a log gives replay and many readers, and one poison message stalls its partition until you route it out.

How it works

Same producer, two brokers. On the left the broker owns each message's state; on the right each group owns a position.

A queue answers "who does this job?"; a log answers "who needs to know this happened?".

Rule What actually happens
At-least-once Ack after processing, and a crash before the ack redelivers. Ack before, and a crash loses the message. The ack itself can be lost, so dedupe on a message id.
Exactly-once Holds only inside Kafka, where output and offset commit together; outside it, see the pitfall in sync vs async.
Ordering Strict within a partition key or FIFO message group; parallelism is capped at the partition or active-group count, and one hot key is one consumer's problem.
Backlog It grows at arrival minus consumption; the arithmetic is owned by sync vs async. Alert on age, not depth.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): SQS, RabbitMQ and Kafka all document at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers.
  • Changed in Kafka 4.2 (Feb 2026): share groups (KIP-932) are production-ready: consumers share partitions, ack per record and count delivery attempts. Queue semantics now exist on a log; 4.1 shipped them as a preview.
  • What's next and what won't change: brokers keep adding the other shape's features. At-least-once and per-key ordering stay true.

On the wire

Break it: a visibility timeout shorter than the work. A model of the broker's timer with two workers (Python 3.15, run 22 Nov 2026):

VIS, WORK = 0.5, 0.8                     # seconds: timeout < processing time
def receive():                           # broker: hand out a visible message and hide it for VIS
    for m, t in queue.items():
        if t <= time.time(): queue[m] = time.time() + VIS; return m
def worker(name):
    m = receive()
    if m: time.sleep(WORK); done.append((name, m)); queue.pop(m, None)   # delete after work
# look for: both workers process m1
# naive belief predicts: one worker owns the message until it finishes

Result: [('w1', 'm1'), ('w2', 'm1')]. The broker can't tell slow from dead: extend the timeout while working (ChangeMessageVisibility).

Measure it

  • See it: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group G shows lag per partition; the SQS console shows messages in flight. Correct is lag near zero and stable.
  • In production: per consumer group, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage or offset lag, receive count above 1, and DLQ arrivals. Rising age with flat depth means one stuck partition or poison message.
  • Bounded by: poison messages and duplicates → maxReceiveCount to a DLQ with an owner and an alarm, idempotent consumers keyed on the message id (idempotency keys).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A queue is destructive: one competing consumer gets each message, the broker hides it for a visibility timeout, ack deletes it, and repeated failures go to a DLQ. A log retains: consumer groups read at their own offsets and can replay. Both are at-least-once, so consumers are idempotent, and both order only per partition or message group. Pick a queue for jobs, a log for facts with many readers.

Q · Mechanism — Why is a duplicate guaranteed eventually, even with a healthy broker? Because the consumer must choose when to ack. After processing, a crash between the side effect and the ack redelivers; before processing, a crash loses the message. There is no third order across a network, since the ack can be lost too. A visibility timeout shorter than the work creates duplicates without any crash, as the Break it shows. So dedupe on a message or event id at the side effect, inside the same transaction when the side effect is a database write.

Q · Trade-off — Ordering matters. What does it cost? Your parallelism ceiling becomes the partition count, and one large customer's key lands on one consumer that no scaling can help. Kafka keeps per-partition order with one consumer per partition per group; SQS FIFO does it per message group. The cheaper move is to need less order: put a version on each message and apply only newer ones. Order by key only where the domain has a real per-entity sequence, such as an account's ledger.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
SQS visibility timeout default 30 s, max 12 h extending doesn't reset the 12 h limit default (as of Nov 2026): SQS docs
SQS retention default 4 days, 60 s to 14 days set the DLQ's longer than the source's default (as of Nov 2026): SQS quotas
SQS FIFO dedup window 5 min a resend inside it adds no duplicate default (as of Nov 2026): SQS FIFO
Kafka retention log.retention.hours = 168 (7 days) broker default, per topic override default: Kafka 4.4 broker configs

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: a queue vs a log
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "messaging", both sit behind a broker, and Kafka now has share groups.
    ↳ Difference: a queue tracks each message and deletes it on ack; a log tracks positions and keeps the messages for every group.
    ↳ Think instead: one job for one worker, or one fact for many readers? Replay needs a log.
  • Don't alert on queue depth.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: depth is the number on the console, and big feels bad.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a million messages draining fast is fine; ten thousand that stopped moving is an outage, and depth can't tell them apart.
    ↳ Do instead: alert on oldest-message age per consumer group, which is the staleness users see.
  • Don't give a standard SQS DLQ the source's retention.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: matching settings looks tidy.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a standard queue keeps the original enqueue time, so a message that spent a day in the source dies a day early in the DLQ, before anyone looks.
    ↳ Do instead: set the DLQ retention longer than the source's, and page someone on its first message.
  • Don't ask for global ordering.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "process events in order" sounds like correctness.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it means one partition and one consumer, a ceiling no hardware lifts.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: order per key, or version each message and drop stale ones.
  • Shelf life: delivery semantics are durable; SQS limits and Kafka's share-group feature are what will move.

Connections

Path:sync vs asyncwebhooksqueues and event streamslong-running jobs
  • Builds on sync vs async: the fork that leads here, the outbox that feeds it and the backlog arithmetic.
  • Bounded by idempotency keys: what at-least-once requires of every consumer.
  • Owned elsewhere: replication and consensus behind the broker live in 03-hld; queueing theory owns Little's Law.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: queue or log for a service boundary.
  • Drilled in Kafka consumer crash before commit.

notes.title: Sync vs Async — Request/Response, Queue, Event-Driven
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §15.3.3: 202 Accepted · AWS Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs · Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures · Apache Kafka 4.4: Design, message delivery semantics

TL;DR

A synchronous call puts the callee's availability, latency and capacity inside yours; a queue or event turns the callee's bad hour into a backlog instead of your error rate. Async doesn't remove failure, it makes it quiet: you trade a loud 5xx for staleness that every dashboard shows as green unless you watch lag. Sync only what the user's answer depends on.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:POST /orderspayment authorise (sync, the answer depends on it)order + outbox row, one transaction201 to the userrelay publishes OrderPlacedemail, search, analytics read at their own pacealert on lag per consumer

Recall

Prompt Answer
What three things does a sync call couple? Availability, latency, and capacity: your threads wait on theirs.
The one question that decides sync or async? Does the caller need the result to answer the user truthfully?
Queue vs event, in one line? A queue is work for one consumer; an event is a fact for any number.
Five sync hops at 99.9 % each? 99.5 %, about 44 hours down a year instead of 9.
What fixes "row written, event never published"? A transactional outbox: the event row commits with the business row.
Draw by hand: an order with sync payment and async consumers User → order service → payment; one transaction with outbox; 201; relay → bus → consumers.

The idea

Checkout calls payment, inventory, email, analytics and the search indexer in a row before answering. The search cluster has a slow minute, the order service's workers all park waiting on it, and orders start failing with 504s, for a reason that has nothing to do with taking money. Then someone moves the work to "write the order, then publish an event", a pod is killed between the two lines, and some orders never reach the warehouse.

The fix splits one business operation by what the user's answer depends on. Payment and the inventory hold stay synchronous, because "your order is placed" is false if either failed. The order row and an OrderPlaced row go into the database in one transaction; a relay publishes the event afterwards. Email, analytics and search subscribe, so the order service doesn't know they exist, and a broken indexer makes search stale instead of making checkout fail.

The trade: async moves a dependency's failure off your error rate and into a backlog, and you pay with a broker, idempotent consumers, a dead-letter path and a lag alarm, because nothing else will tell you it broke.

How it works

One order, split at the point where the user's answer is decided. ① and ② are on the user's clock; ③ and ④ are not.

Everything after 201 can fail for hours without making the answer untrue, which is the test for what belongs on the critical path.

Shape What happens, and who acts
Sync request/response The caller holds a thread and a connection until the callee answers or a timeout fires; their p99 is inside yours. Bounded by the timeout hierarchy and bulkheads.
Accept, then process 202 Accepted + a status resource: honest now, done later. Owned by long-running jobs.
Queue One consumer does each unit of work; the broker redelivers on failure and parks poison messages in a DLQ. Owned by queues and event streams.
Event stream A fact any number of consumer groups read at their own offsets; adding a consumer doesn't touch the producer.
The middle The broker absorbs bursts and holds the backlog; the relay turns a committed row into a message, at least once.

The two numbers that make sync expensive and async dangerous:

availability, sync chain = a^n = 0.999^5 ≈ 0.995        ← 5 hops, each 99.9 %
downtime/year ≈ 0.005 · 8,760 h ≈ 44 h, vs 8.8 h for one hop
backlog grows at λ − μ when arrivals λ beat consumption μ   ← it never drains by waiting
recovery = B ÷ (μ − λ) = 43,200 ÷ (40 − 6) ≈ 21 min      ← 2 h stuck at 6/s, then 40/s drain

Evolution

Lineage:2011 Apache Kafka open-sourced (a retained log)2017 Kafka 0.11 (Jun): idempotent producer and transactions2022 RFC 9110 restates 202 Accepted2026 Kafka 4.2 (Feb): share groups, queue semantics on a log
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the sync/async split, the outbox and at-least-once delivery are standard practice, and every major broker documents idempotent consumers.
  • Changed in Kafka 4.2 (Feb 2026): share groups (KIP-932) are production-ready, with per-record acknowledgement and delivery counts, so "queue or log" is now partly a consumer-group choice on one broker, not only a choice of product.
  • What's next and what won't change: brokers keep blurring queue and log. The fork itself, "does the user's answer depend on this?", and the at-least-once rule don't move.

On the wire

The outbox as one SQLite transaction plus the relay loop, trimmed from the model below (Python 3.15, run 22 Nov 2026):

with db:                                   # ② one transaction: both rows, or neither
    db.execute("insert into orders values(?)", (order_id,))
    db.execute("insert into outbox(id) values(?)", (order_id,))
# relay, a separate loop: publish first, then mark sent
for rowid, oid in db.execute("select rowid, id from outbox where sent = 0 limit 50"):
    bus.publish("OrderPlaced", oid)        # ③ a crash here, before the mark...
    with db:
        db.execute("update outbox set sent = 1 where rowid = ?", (rowid,))
# ...means the next pass publishes again: duplicates, never loss → consumers dedupe on the event id

Break it: write the order, then publish, with a 2 % chance of a crash between the two steps; then the same orders through the outbox.

for i in range(1000):
    with db: db.execute("insert into orders values(?)", (i,))   # committed
    if random.random() < 0.02: continue                          # pod killed before publish
    bus.append(i)
print("lost =", 1000 - len(set(bus)))
# look for: dual write loses events for orders that exist; the outbox loses none and duplicates some
# naive belief predicts: lost = 0, because the publish is the very next line

Run on Python 3.15 with seed 7: dual write lost 23 of 1,000 events with no duplicates; the outbox lost 0 and published 27 duplicates. So the outbox converts loss, which you can't detect, into duplicates, which an idempotent consumer absorbs.

Measure it

  • See it: per consumer group, lag in messages and the age of the oldest unprocessed one (ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage on SQS, offset lag on Kafka); correct is flat and seconds old while producers run.
  • In production: oldest-message age per consumer, not queue depth, plus unsent outbox rows. Age climbing while the order path's error rate stays zero is the async failure in its natural form.
  • Bounded by: a silent backlog or lost events → per-consumer age alarms, a DLQ with an owner, the outbox, idempotent consumers (idempotency keys); a sync cascade → timeouts and bulkheads.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The deciding question is whether the caller needs the result to answer truthfully. If yes, it's sync, and you bound it with timeouts and bulkheads because their availability and tail become yours. If not, publish it: a queue for one worker, an event for many. That turns their outage into a backlog. The price is at-least-once delivery, so idempotent consumers, an outbox so events aren't lost, and alerting on oldest-message age.

Q · Mechanism — What does a synchronous call actually couple you to? Three things. Availability multiplies: five hops at 99.9 % give 99.5 %. Latency adds and the tail amplifies with fan-out (tail latency owns the p^n arithmetic). The one people miss is capacity: a caller holds a thread or connection while it waits, so a slow dependency eats your concurrency and you stop serving requests that never touch it. That's the cascade, and timeouts and bulkheads exist to cap exactly that resource (cascading failures).

Q · Trade-off — When is a queue worse than a synchronous call? When the user is waiting for the answer. A queue in front of a login or a price check moves the wait somewhere unobservable and adds a status problem you then solve anyway. It also hides backpressure: the producer never learns the consumer is struggling. Pick async when the caller only needs the work to happen eventually, and 202 plus a job resource when it needs an acknowledgement now and a result later.

Q · Failure — Search results are two hours stale and every dashboard is green. What happened? A consumer stopped, and nothing on the order path can see it: no 5xx, no latency change. The resource running out is the consumer's throughput, and the symptom is oldest-message age per group. Confirm with lag per consumer group, then check what limits μ: if it's the search cluster's write rate, more consumers make it worse. Fix the consumer, raise μ above λ, and recovery is B ÷ (μ − λ), about 21 minutes in the derivation above.

Q · Design — An order touches payment, inventory, email, analytics and search. Which are sync? The binding constraint is what you can truthfully tell the user at the click. Payment authorisation and the inventory hold are sync, with tight timeouts, because the answer depends on them. The order and an outbox row commit together; one OrderPlaced event feeds email, analytics and search as separate consumer groups, so adding a fourth is a subscription, not a change to checkout. The first signal I'd watch is oldest-message age per consumer group, because a broken indexer is invisible from checkout. The service-boundary choice lives in service communication patterns.

Compare

Shape Caller gets Failure looks like Must also build When you'd pick it
Sync the answer now errors and timeouts, loud timeouts, bulkheads, retries with jitter the answer depends on it
202 + job an id now, the result later jobs stuck non-terminal status resource, reaper slow work the caller tracks
Queue nothing back backlog, a DLQ filling idempotent worker, DLQ owner one worker, eventually
Event nothing back one consumer's lag grows outbox, per-group lag alarm many independent reactions

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Sync chain availability a^n; 99.5 % for 5 × 99.9 % about 44 h/year down vs 8.8 h derived
Recovery from backlog B B ÷ (μ − λ) ≈ 21 min B = 43,200, μ = 40/s, λ = 6/s derived
Accepted, not complete 202 + Location the sync-to-async bridge in HTTP spec: RFC 9110 §15.3.3
Dual write vs outbox, 2 % crash 23 lost vs 0 lost, 27 duplicates 1,000 orders, seed 7 measured: Python 3.15 model, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Async is more resilient, so default to it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a queue keeps accepting work when the consumer is down, and that looks like availability.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the failure is still there, as staleness and backlog that can run for hours with every dashboard green. You traded a loud failure for a silent one.
    ↳ Think instead: async is a good trade only when you watch the quiet signal: oldest-message age per consumer.
  • Not the same: a queue vs an event stream
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both sit on a broker and both deliver at least once.
    ↳ Difference: a queue hands each message to one competing consumer and deletes it on ack. An event is retained, and every consumer group reads all of it at its own offset.
    ↳ Think instead: work for one, or a fact for many? Replay and future consumers point at a log.
  • Don't write the row and then publish the event.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: two lines, one after the other, and it works in every test.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a crash between them leaves orders with no event: 23 of 1,000 in the Break it at a 2 % crash rate, and nothing reports it.
    ↳ Do instead: commit an outbox row in the same transaction and let a relay publish it; consumers dedupe the duplicates.
  • Don't put a queue in front of a user waiting for the answer.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "async scales better" is the slogan, and the queue absorbs spikes.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the user still waits, now with no timeout they can see, and you add a status endpoint, polling and a DLQ to answer a question a sync call answered.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: a sync call with a tight timeout, or 202 and a job resource when the work is genuinely slow.
  • "Our broker has exactly-once, so consumers needn't be idempotent"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: Kafka documents exactly-once semantics, and the phrase sounds end to end.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it holds where the output and the consumer's offset commit together inside Kafka. Kafka's own design notes say writing to an external system needs that position stored with the output.
    ↳ Think instead: at-least-once plus idempotency whenever the side effect leaves the broker.
  • Shelf life: the fork and the arithmetic are durable. Broker features, such as Kafka's share groups, keep moving the line between queue and log.

Connections

Path:sync vs asyncRESTwebhooksqueues and event streamslong-running jobs
  • Owned elsewhere: queues owns delivery semantics, ordering and DLQs; long-running jobs owns 202 and the job resource.
  • Bounded by the timeout hierarchy on the sync side and idempotency keys on the async side.
  • Composes with webhooks: the async push to systems you don't run.
  • Decided in service communication patterns; sagas for cross-service atomicity in data patterns.
  • Drilled in order and event outbox.

notes.title: Long-Running Jobs over HTTP — 202 + Polling vs Callback vs Streaming
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110 §15.3.3: 202 Accepted · 📜 RFC 9110 §10.2.3: Retry-After · 📜 RFC 9457: Problem Details · AWS: ALB attributes (idle timeout) · nginx: proxy_read_timeout · Claude: Message Batches

TL;DR

When work outlasts a request, stop holding the connection and make the job a resource: POST returns 202 with a Location to poll and a Retry-After that sets the pace. Every request is then milliseconds long, so no load balancer, proxy or SDK timeout in the middle gets a vote. The price is a job store, a status endpoint, and polling load you must bound yourself.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:POST /jobs + Idempotency-Keyjob row queued, enqueue202 + Location + Retry-AfterGET /jobs/j1200 running, Retry-After growsworker sets succeedednext poll returns a result linkGET result

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does 202 promise? Accepted for processing, not completed. It might never run (RFC 9110 §15.3.3).
Two headers that make 202 usable? Location to the status resource, Retry-After for the poll pace.
Who in the middle kills a held request first? The load balancer: AWS ALB idle timeout defaults to 60 s.
Why an idempotency key on submit? A retry after a lost 202 otherwise starts a second, billed job.
Polls for a 22-min job at a fixed 2 s? 660; doubling to a 60 s cap needs 27.
Draw by hand: a submit whose 202 is lost, then polling POST+key → job row → 202 lost → same POST → same job → GET → running → done.

The idea

A report export takes four minutes. The first design holds POST /exports open until the file is ready. At 60 s the ALB closes the idle connection and the client gets a 504, while the worker carries on. The client can't tell whether the export happened, so it retries, and now two exports run. The user saw an error, and you paid twice.

The job pattern changes the same request. POST /exports writes a job row, enqueues it and answers in milliseconds with 202, Location: /exports/j1 and Retry-After: 2. The client polls that resource, and the server slows the polling as the job ages. The submit carries an Idempotency-Key, so a retried submit whose 202 was lost finds the same row and gets the same job back. No hop ever sees a request longer than a few milliseconds, so no timeout in the middle can fire.

The trade: the job survives every timeout you don't control, and you pay with a second resource, a store, a worker fleet and a poll stream you must throttle.

How it works

One submit whose response is lost, the retry that finds the same job, then polling. All arrows pass the balancer; only the first is drawn through it.

The key turns "did my submit work?" from an unanswerable question into a lookup. The contract itself is the job's state machine, not the endpoints:

Terminal states are terminal: a client that sees succeeded never polls again.

Rule What actually happens
The middle stops mattering The LB's idle timeout and nginx's proxy_read_timeout (both 60 s by default) only cut requests that stay open; job requests never do.
Retry-After is the server's throttle RFC 9110 defines its meaning for 503 and 3xx; on 202 and a running status it's a widely used convention, honoured only by clients you write or document.
Results live apart from the job The job record is small and kept for audit; the output gets its own URL and an expires_at.
A reaper owns stuck jobs A job past its maximum duration moves to failed with an RFC 9457 problem body, so no client polls forever.

Polling cost is arithmetic, and the growing interval is what makes it affordable:

fixed: D / T = 1,320 s / 2 s = 660 polls                ← a 22-minute job, polled every 2 s
doubling 1, 2, 4 … 32 s = 63 s in 6 polls               ← then capped at 60 s
capped: ⌈1,257 / 60⌉ = 21 more → 27 polls, lag ≤ 60 s  ← completion noticed up to one interval late
fleet: J / T = 10,000 jobs / 2 s = 5,000 status rps     ← vs 10,000 / 60 ≈ 167 rps at the cap

Evolution

Lineage:1999 202 in HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616)2012 429 + Retry-After (RFC 6585)2022 RFC 9110 restates both2023 problem details (RFC 9457, obsoletes 7807)
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026). LLM batch APIs follow the shape: Claude's Message Batches return a batch you poll for processing_status and download from results_url.
  • What's next: the Idempotency-Key header is an IETF draft (draft-09), not yet an RFC. What won't change: a request can't say "still working", so slow work becomes a resource.

On the wire

Captured on 22 Nov 2026 from a 25-line http.server job API (our code) on 127.0.0.1, Python 3.15, curl 8.7.1; Date, Server and Content-Length trimmed:

POST /jobs   Idempotency-Key: 5f2c   {"input":"prompts.jsonl"}    # ① submit
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Location: /jobs/j1                     # the status resource: the whole contract hangs off it
Retry-After: 1                         # the server sets the pace, not the client
{"id": "j1", "state": "queued"}

GET /jobs/j1                                                      # ③ poll
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Retry-After: 2                         # grows as the job ages
{"id": "j1", "state": "running"}

GET /jobs/j1                                                      # ④ poll after completion
HTTP/1.1 200 OK                        # no Retry-After: terminal, stop polling
{"id": "j1", "state": "succeeded", "result": "/jobs/j1/result"}

Break it: a lost 202 is indistinguishable from a failed submit, so the client must retry. Against the same server:

def submit(key, read=True):                     # read=False: the 202 never reaches us
    c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", 8099)
    c.request("POST", "/jobs", body=b"{}", headers={"Idempotency-Key": key} if key else {})
    r = c.getresponse(); body = r.read(); c.close()   # the server has created the job either way
    return json.loads(body)["id"] if read else None
submit(None, read=False); submit(None)          # retry, no key
submit("5f2c", read=False); submit("5f2c")      # retry, same key
# look for: two jobs without the key, one with it
# naive belief predicts: one job both times, because "the first request failed"

Run on Python 3.15: no key: 2 jobs, with key: 1 job. The server can't tell a lost response from a new request; only the key can.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i on the submit shows 202, Location and Retry-After; repeating it with the same Idempotency-Key returns the same job id, and polls show Retry-After growing.
  • In production: per job type, polls per job (rising means clients ignore Retry-After), duplicate submits caught by the key, and jobs non-terminal past their maximum duration.
  • Bounded by: duplicate expensive work → idempotent submit (idempotency keys). Status-read storms → growing Retry-After, cached state, 429 (rate limiting). Stuck jobs → a reaper with a per-type timeout.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: When work outlasts a request, I make the job a resource. The submit is idempotent and returns 202 with a Location and a Retry-After. The client polls a status resource with an explicit state machine and follows a link to the result. Every request is short, so the LB's 60-second idle timeout never fires. Callbacks and streaming are extra views of the same job, not separate implementations.

Q · Mechanism — Why not just raise the load balancer timeout to five minutes? Because the LB is only the first hop with an opinion: nginx, a CDN and the client SDK each cut a held request at their own limit, since it looks hung to all of them. When one fires, the client gets a 504 while the work continues, so it retries and doubles the work. Each held request also pins a worker slot for minutes. Making the job a resource removes the ambiguity.

Q · Trade-off — Polling, callback or streaming? Polling is the default because it works for every client: no inbound reachability, and a crashed client just polls again. Its cost is reads and up to one interval of lag. A callback (webhooks) is immediate but drags in signing, retries, a DLQ and an SSRF review, so offer it to server clients at volume. Stream (SSE) only when partial output has value, like tokens or rows. For an atomic PDF there's nothing to stream but a percentage.

Q · Failure — Database load climbs during an incident, and most queries are job status reads. What's happening? Status load scales with in-flight jobs, and jobs pile up when workers slow down. So polling rises exactly when the store can least afford it. Confirm it with polls per job and status reads per second plotted against queue depth: if they rise together and clients ignore Retry-After, you've found the loop. Fix it by serving job state from a cache with a short TTL, growing Retry-After, and answering 429 to clients that ignore it.

Q · Design — Design the job API for LLM batch work that runs for minutes to hours and is costly to re-run. The binding constraint is cost: a duplicate is GPU time billed twice. So the submit requires an idempotency key that maps to the job id. The path is client → gateway → API → job store → queue → workers, plus object storage for results with an expires_at, because a gigabyte output isn't kept as long as its job record. Delivery is polling by default, SSE on the job for token output, and an optional signed callback. Watch first: jobs non-terminal past their expected duration, the failure that never errors. Placement is decided in service communication patterns.

Compare

202 + polling Callback SSE on the job Hold the request
Client must be reachable no yes, publicly no no
Completion noticed up to one interval late at once at once, with partial output at once, if it survives
When you'd pick it the default, every client server clients at volume tokens, rows, progress work that finishes well under every timeout

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
202 Accepted accepted, not completed may never be acted on spec: RFC 9110 §15.3.3
Retry-After seconds or an HTTP-date meaning defined for 503, 3xx; 429 in RFC 6585 spec: RFC 9110 §10.2.3
ALB idle timeout 60 s the first hop that cuts a held request default (as of Nov 2026): AWS ALB docs
nginx proxy_read_timeout 60 s the next hop, if the LB is raised default (as of Nov 2026): nginx docs
Polls, 22-min job 660 fixed at 2 s · 27 doubling to 60 s lag ≤ 60 s at the cap derived
Claude Message Batches results within 24 h or the batch expires; kept 29 days an LLM job API's retention contract default (as of Nov 2026): Claude docs

Pitfalls

  • "202 means the work has started"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's a 2xx, and success codes feel like success.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: RFC 9110 says the request "might or might not eventually be acted upon". It may sit queued, or be rejected later by a validator.
    ↳ Think instead: 202 is a handle, not a result. Without a Location to query, the client has been told nothing.
  • Not the same: idempotency key vs Retry-After
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both appear in "make retries safe" discussions of the same endpoint.
    ↳ Difference: the key makes a repeated submit return the same job. Retry-After paces repeated reads of the status.
    ↳ Think instead: the key protects your bill; Retry-After protects your database. A job API needs both.
  • Don't fix a 504 by raising the LB timeout.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's one setting, and the error goes away in testing.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the next hop (nginx, CDN, SDK) still cuts at its own limit, and every held request pins a worker for minutes.
    ↳ Do instead: make the job a resource. Raise timeouts only for streams that send data regularly.
  • Don't build a job API for work that finishes in under a second.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one async pattern everywhere looks consistent.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a job row, a queue hop and a second round trip cost the client more than the wait, and add a store to operate.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: return the answer synchronously, and switch when p99 nears the smallest timeout on the path.
  • "Polling cost grows with the log of job duration"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a doubling interval sounds logarithmic.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: only until the cap. After that it is linear again: a 22-minute job spends 21 of its 27 polls at the 60 s cap.
    ↳ Think instead: the cap sets the cost and the lag together. Pick it from how late completion may be noticed.
  • Don't ship without a stuck-job reaper.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: workers either succeed or throw, so every job seems to end.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a worker killed mid-job leaves the row running forever. Clients poll forever, and no error or alert ever fires.
    ↳ Do instead: give each job type a maximum duration, and move overdue jobs to failed with a problem body.
  • Shelf life: the pattern and the arithmetic are durable. LB and vendor defaults move, and Idempotency-Key may become an RFC.

Connections

Path:sync vs asynclong-running jobswebhooksAI-stack protocols
  • Builds on sync vs async: this is the async fork, exposed over HTTP.
  • Owned elsewhere: choosing the right code owns 202 vs 200 vs 303; idempotency keys owns the key's storage.
  • Bounded by rate limiting: 429 for clients that ignore Retry-After.
  • Composes with queues: what carries the work behind the job resource.
  • Contrasts with streaming LLM tokens: when partial output is the product.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: where a boundary goes async.

notes.title: Server Protocols in the AI Stack — HTTP + SSE, MCP, A2A
notes.html:
References

MCP 2026-07-28: Streamable HTTP · A2A Protocol Specification (1.0.0) · Claude: Streaming messages · WHATWG HTML: Server-sent events

TL;DR

The AI stack invented no wire format: a model call is an HTTP POST whose streamed reply is SSE, MCP is JSON-RPC over stdio or one HTTP endpoint, and A2A is JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON with SSE for progress. So the proxies, balancers and gateways in the middle meet ordinary HTTP, and the failures are ordinary too: buffering, idle timeouts, cancellation that never arrives.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:host POST with stream: true200 text/event-stream deltastool call: POST /mcp with Mcp-Method headerJSON reply, or SSE progress then resultdelegate: A2A SendStreamingMessageSSE task updatesclose stream = cancel

Recall

Prompt Answer
MCP's two transports today? stdio for a local subprocess, Streamable HTTP for a remote server.
Does a remote MCP server need sticky routing? No: since 2026-07-28 there are no sessions, any replica serves any POST.
What keeps a quiet stream alive through an idle timer? SSE comment lines (MCP) or ping events (Claude's stream).

The idea

A team puts a model call behind its gateway. Tokens arrive all at once at the end: the gateway buffers. They fix that, and a long tool call dies at 60 s, the balancer's idle timeout. Then users close the tab and generation keeps running.

None of that is about MCP or A2A. Each is JSON over HTTP with SSE for progress, so each inherits HTTP's middle. What they add is information for it: MCP mirrors method and tool name into headers, and its 2026-07-28 revision removed sessions so a plain balancer works.

The trade: every piece of HTTP infrastructure works unchanged, and you inherit its streaming traps on every hop.

How it works

One agent host, three kinds of outbound call. Each leaves your control at a different place.

Only stdio avoids the network; the rules below apply at the gateway.

Rule What actually happens
Buffering must be off on stream routes A buffering proxy turns token-by-token output into one late delivery; status, bytes and total time look normal (buffering vs streaming proxies).
Idle timers need traffic A 60 s idle timeout cuts a quiet stream. Claude's stream may carry ping events; MCP servers are encouraged to send : comment lines.
No stickiness for MCP Each MCP message is its own POST carrying its protocol version, so any replica answers. A server answers GET with 405.
Route on headers, enforce on the body Gateways read MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name; the server must reject a body that disagrees with them.
Closing the stream is the cancel On Streamable HTTP, closing the response stream cancels the request; through NAT a dead client may send no FIN for a long time.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟡 Maturing (Nov 2026). Provider SSE streaming is settled; MCP's stateless HTTP shape is four months old, and A2A released 1.0.0 with three bindings.
  • Changed in MCP 2026-07-28: sessions (Mcp-Session-Id), the standing GET stream and Last-Event-ID resumption were removed. A balancer that pinned clients for MCP can drop the affinity; a dropped stream now loses its request, so it is re-sent.
  • What's next: HTTP+SSE, MCP's 2024 transport, deprecated since March 2025, is eligible for removal. What won't change: text streams down as SSE; continuous upstream audio needs something else (WebRTC for voice AI).

On the wire

Illustrative: what a gateway sees from the three calls, headers and data: lines trimmed. The MCP request's full body is owned by MCP transports.

POST /v1/messages        {"stream": true, …}          # model call
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream                       # every hop must pass this through unbuffered
event: content_block_delta
event: ping                                           # keeps idle timers from firing
event: message_stop

POST /mcp                                             # remote tool call
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream          # client must accept both reply forms
MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
Mcp-Method: tools/call                                # routable without reading the body
Mcp-Name: get_weather

POST /a2a   SendStreamingMessage                      # delegation, JSON-RPC binding
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream                       # task status and artifact updates

Measure it

  • See it: curl -N against the route: deltas print one by one if nothing buffers; a single burst at the end means a hop is buffering.
  • In production: per route, time to first byte against total time (equal means buffering), streams cut near the idle timeout, generation after client disconnect.
  • Bounded by: a stream cut mid-operation → heartbeats below every idle timeout on the path. A re-sent request after a drop → idempotent tools; anything longer than a stream survives → a job resource.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Nothing in the AI stack needed a new transport. Model APIs are a POST with an SSE reply. MCP is JSON-RPC over stdio locally or one Streamable HTTP endpoint remotely, and since the July 2026 revision it's stateless. A2A is JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON with SSE for task updates. So the real work is the middle: unbuffered streaming routes, heartbeats under idle timeouts, and cancellation you can't rely on.

Q · Mechanism — What does a load balancer or gateway need to do differently for a remote MCP server? Less than before: every message is an independent POST carrying its version, so round-robin works without affinity. Streaming replies need the same treatment as any SSE route: buffering off, an idle timeout above the longest quiet gap or heartbeats. Policy can key on the mirrored Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers without parsing JSON, but the server must still check they match the body, or a client can mislabel a call.

Q · Trade-off — When does SSE stop fitting and something else take over? SSE fits one request followed by a server stream: a completion, a tool call, a task update. It stops fitting when the client streams up continuously too, as in live voice, where interruption couples the directions. That's WebRTC or WebSocket territory, and as of Nov 2026 OpenAI recommends WebRTC even for server-side voice. It also stops when the work outlives any connection: then a job resource, with streaming as an optional view.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
MCP transports 2 stdio and Streamable HTTP; HTTP+SSE only for old servers spec: MCP 2026-07-28
MCP notification accepted 202, no body the job code, reused spec: MCP 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP
A2A bindings 3 JSON-RPC, gRPC, HTTP+JSON; streaming as SSE spec: A2A 1.0.0

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: MCP's HTTP+SSE transport vs an SSE reply on Streamable HTTP
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both contain "SSE", and posts say "SSE is deprecated in MCP".
    ↳ Difference: HTTP+SSE was the 2024 two-endpoint transport, now deprecated. An SSE stream as the reply to one POST is current.
    ↳ Think instead: ask whether there's a standing GET stream. If there is, it's the old transport.
  • "Agent protocols need WebSocket"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: agents feel conversational and long-lived, and "realtime" suggests a socket.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the traffic is a request then a server stream, SSE's shape. MCP, A2A and provider APIs all chose it and kept gateways and logs working.
    ↳ Think instead: one request, one stream down: SSE. Full duplex only when the client streams up continuously.
  • Don't expose a remote MCP server as "just a tool server".
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it started as a local helper.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it's now an internet-facing API with tenancy and abuse potential. The spec requires Origin validation because a local server can be reached by DNS rebinding.
    ↳ Do instead: put it behind the gateway with auth and rate limits, like any API (API authentication).
  • Don't treat a stream as the durable record.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the output is all there on the wire as it's generated.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a dropped stream loses everything not yet received, and MCP 2026-07-28 has no resumption, so the request runs again.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option for output that matters: a job resource with a stored result; stream only as a view of it.
  • Shelf life: SSE is durable; MCP headers, A2A bindings and vendor advice move.

Connections

Path:long-running jobsAI-stack protocolsthe choice framework
  • Owned elsewhere: MCP transports owns messages, _meta and errors; A2A owns task semantics.
  • Builds on server-sent events: the wire format every stream here uses.
  • Bounded by buffering vs streaming proxies: the hop that silently breaks streaming.
  • Used by streaming LLM tokens: the token path end to end.
  • Contrasts with WebRTC for voice AI: when the client streams up too.

notes.title: The API Choice Framework — REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL vs SSE vs WebSocket vs Queue
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics · grpc.io: Core concepts · graphql.org: Performance · 📜 WHATWG HTML §9.2: Server-sent events · AWS Builders' Library: Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs

TL;DR

Four ordered questions pick the shape: does the caller wait, does it fit one request, does it keep flowing, who consumes it. The answer is almost never decided on speed. What actually differs is what the middle can do with the call (cache, retry, inspect), browser reach, the failure mode and the operational weight, and the tiebreak is the lightest option that still meets the requirement.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:caller waits?queue, event or webhookfits one request?202 + jobkeeps flowing?SSE or WebSocketwho consumes?REST · gRPC · GraphQLtiebreak: lowest operational weight

Recall

Prompt Answer
The first question, before any protocol name? Does the caller need the result to continue? It decides the failure mode.
Which options can't a browser call directly? gRPC (needs gRPC-Web and a proxy) and brokers.
Which option lets a shared HTTP cache act unchanged? REST. GraphQL only with GET or persisted queries; gRPC never.
What makes gRPC the answer, in one word? The schema: codegen and an enforced contract across teams and languages.
Who in the middle can act on a POST /graphql? Almost nobody: one URL, one method, the meaning is in the body.
Draw by hand: the decision tree Waits? no → queue. One request? no → job. Flowing? yes → stream. Consumer → REST, gRPC, GraphQL.

The idea

Five decisions, each run through the questions in order:

  • "Send the confirmation email after checkout." Waits? No. → an event on a bus, idempotent consumer, DLQ. Defence: email being down must never make checkout fail.
  • "Checkout must reserve inventory first." Waits? Yes; one request; not flowing; internal caller. → gRPC with a deadline. Defence: it's on the critical path by necessity, so bound it and keep a degraded path.
  • "Stream the assistant's answer into the chat UI." Waits; flowing; the client sends nothing upward mid-turn. → SSE. Defence: plain HTTP keeps the existing auth and edge; WebSocket's weight buys nothing here.
  • "A partner wants to know when an order ships." The partner isn't waiting on a call, and runs a backend you don't. → a signed webhook with retries and a polling endpoint as fallback.
  • "The home screen needs user, orders and recommendations." Waits; one request; not flowing; consumer is your own apps. Several clients wanting different fields → GraphQL; one client → REST with one compound endpoint. Defence: the round trips are the constraint, and a view endpoint fixes them without handing out a query planner.

The trade: the framework stops a design anchoring on a technology name, and you pay by deciding on failure mode and operational weight, which no benchmark shows.

How it works

This note owns the tree; the chapter map links it. The binding question comes first, and plain REST is the default leaf that every other leaf must earn its way past.

Each leaf, and the one condition that would change it:

  • Queue or event (queues, webhooks): a user waiting on screen for the result; then it's a job with a status.
  • 202 + job (long-running jobs): partial output is the product, as with tokens; then stream it.
  • SSE or WebSocket (choosing a realtime transport): updates are rare; a poll is simpler.
  • REST (REST): one screen needs many resources over a slow link and parallel fetches aren't enough.
  • gRPC (gRPC): a browser must call it directly; then gRPC-Web and a proxy, or REST at the edge.
  • GraphQL (GraphQL): the clients are few and their shapes stable; compound REST views are cheaper to run.

The full matrix, durable facts only:

REST gRPC GraphQL SSE WebSocket Queue or log
Caller waits yes yes yes streams it streams it no
Shape request/response unary + 3 streaming types query/response server push full duplex fire and forget
Browser reach native gRPC-Web + proxy native native native not directly
Contract OpenAPI, can drift .proto, compiled schema, introspectable none none optional registry
Shared HTTP cache yes, per resource no GET or persisted only n/a no n/a
Who in the middle acts CDN, cache, gateway, retrying client an L7 proxy or mesh, per stream a gateway, little else a proxy that must not buffer an LB that must allow long idle the broker
Failure presents as an error to the caller an error or DEADLINE_EXCEEDED partial data + errors a dropped stream a dropped socket backlog and lag
Backpressure 429/503 HTTP/2 flow control rejection by cost transport flow control none above TCP consumer pull rate
Debug with curl grpcurl GraphQL tooling curl -N a WS client broker tooling

Tiebreak, lightest to heaviest operational weight (a judgment, not a measurement): REST < SSE < GraphQL ≈ gRPC < queue < WebSocket. Capability rarely decides between two options that both work; the weight you carry for years does.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): every leaf of the tree is a settled standard or de-facto practice; the cross-topic arc is in the chapter map's Lineage.
  • Changed in RFC 10008 (Jun 2026): QUERY gives REST a safe, cacheable request with a body, which removes one reason to reach for POST /search or GraphQL. The GraphQL-over-HTTP working draft (Nov 2026) blesses GET for queries, which narrows GraphQL's caching gap.
  • What's next: QUERY support in proxies, and OpenAI-style APIs offering WebRTC and WebSocket beside SSE. What won't change: who waits and who consumes decide the shape.

On the wire

Illustrative: the same "get order 8f2" in three styles, showing what a cache or proxy in the middle can read without your docs.

GET /orders/8f2                         # REST: method + URL say "safe read of one thing"
Accept: application/json                #   → a shared cache may key on the URL and reuse it

POST /graphql                           # GraphQL: one URL, one method for every operation
Content-Type: application/json          #   → the meaning is in the body; a cache sees a POST
{"query": "{ order(id: \"8f2\") { id status } }"}

POST /shop.v1.Orders/GetOrder           # gRPC: the path names the method
content-type: application/grpc          #   → an L7 proxy can route per method, never cache
te: trailers                            #   status arrives later, as grpc-status in trailers

Break it: "pick gRPC because binary encoding is faster". Encoding against one hop, on 127.0.0.1:

import json, pickle, time                           # pickle: a binary stand-in for protobuf
order = {"id": "8f2", "items": [{"sku": f"S{i}", "qty": i, "price": 9.99} for i in range(20)]}
def per_op(fn, n=20000):
    t = time.perf_counter(); [fn() for _ in range(n)]; return (time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1e6
js = per_op(lambda: json.loads(json.dumps(order)))
bn = per_op(lambda: pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(order)))
hop_us, db_us = 147.9, 5000                          # hop: measured loopback HTTP GET; db: assumed
print(f"json {js:.1f} us, binary {bn:.1f} us, saved {100*(js-bn)/(hop_us+db_us):.2f}% of one call")
# look for: the share of one call's time the binary encoding saves
# naive belief predicts: a large share, because "binary is faster"

Run twice on Python 3.15 (22 Nov 2026), a 924-byte order: JSON 15–23 µs, binary 8–13 µs, one loopback HTTP hop 147.9 µs (measured separately). Against that hop plus an assumed 5 ms database call, the binary encoding saves 0.15–0.18%. It is real only at very high message rates; the choice is made on the rows above.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i on a REST read shows Cache-Control and an ETag; the same read through GraphQL shows a POST the CDN logs as a miss; grpcurl shows the deadline and status.
  • In production: per interface, CDN hit ratio, error rate by status, oldest-message age on queues, open connections on streams. Count distinct protocols per org: each one past two duplicates auth, retries, tracing and rate limits.
  • Bounded by: a protocol choice nobody can operate → one default per consumer type in an ADR, exceptions argued, and one shared story for auth, tracing and retries that every protocol must implement.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Six options, four ordered questions. Does the caller need the result? If not, it's a queue or an event. Does it fit one request? If not, a job. Does it keep flowing? Then SSE or WebSocket. Otherwise the consumer decides: REST for browsers and partners, gRPC inside, GraphQL for many first-party UIs. Speed rarely decides; cacheability, browser reach, failure mode and operational weight do.

Q · Mechanism — Why does sync-or-async come before the protocol? Because it decides the failure mode, and you live with that. A synchronous call couples you to the callee's availability and latency: availabilities multiply, so five hops at 99.9% leave about 99.5% (sync vs async owns the arithmetic). An asynchronous hand-off turns the same outage into a backlog: nothing errors, everything is late. No protocol changes that: gRPC with a deadline is still coupling, a queue behind an HTTP submit is still async. REST against gRPC then changes codegen and caching, not your outage story.

Q · Trade-off — GraphQL removes round trips. Why isn't it the default for public APIs? Because it moves costs rather than removing them. One request returns exactly a screen's fields, which wins for mobile clients on slow links. But queries arrive as a POST with a body per client, so the CDN offload REST gets per URL is gone, and the client composes the query's cost. For untrusted callers that means an allow-list of persisted queries, at which point you've rebuilt a fixed set of endpoints with extra machinery. The tipping point is real client diversity, first-party.

Q · Failure — The org runs all six. What breaks first? The cross-cutting story, not a protocol. Auth is a bearer token here, mTLS there, an HMAC on webhooks; retries live in a gRPC client, a REST gateway and the broker; traceparent crosses HTTP but someone forgot the message header, so traces stop at the queue. What runs out is the team's capacity to keep several operational models correct. You'd confirm it with traces broken at a protocol seam and incidents that start with "which system is this". The fix is a default per consumer type and one shared story per concern.

Q · Design — Set the API strategy for a web app, mobile apps, partners and forty internal services. The binding constraint is four consumer classes with different needs, so one protocol is a compromise on all of them. REST with OpenAPI at the public edge, because every integrator's tooling speaks it; gRPC inside, where forty services in several languages pay for codegen and propagated deadlines; SSE for streams to browsers; events where nobody waits. One gateway translates edge to internal, one repository holds .proto and OpenAPI with breaking-change checks. Watch first the seam where a request crosses protocols and loses trace context (service communication patterns).

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
gRPC call types 4 unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, bidirectional spec: grpc.io core concepts
SSE payload encoding UTF-8 only binary has to be base64-encoded spec: WHATWG HTML §9.2
GraphQL mutation over GET 405 GET is for queries only spec: GraphQL over HTTP, working draft (Nov 2026)
Sync chain of 5 at 99.9% ≈ 99.5% a^n, owned by sync vs async derived
JSON vs binary encode + decode, 924 B 15–23 µs vs 8–13 µs against a 147.9 µs loopback HTTP hop measured: Python 3.15, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Pick the protocol by performance"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: benchmarks are easy to find and binary formats sound fast.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the Break it shows encoding saving under 0.2% of one call once a hop and a database call are counted. Database and downstream time dominate almost every service.
    ↳ Think instead: decide on contract, cacheability, browser reach, failure mode and weight, and bring numbers only when message rates are very high.
  • Not the same: a queue vs a log
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "async messaging" and both sit behind a broker.
    ↳ Difference: a queue hands each message to one competing consumer and deletes it; a log keeps it, and many consumer groups read at their own offsets and can replay.
    ↳ Think instead: work to be done once → queue; a fact many teams read, now or next year → log.
  • "GraphQL replaces REST"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it fixes REST's best-known weakness, round trips per screen.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it gives up per-URL HTTP caching and hands the client control of query cost, so a public endpoint needs persisted queries and cost limits.
    ↳ Think instead: GraphQL for many first-party clients, REST for public and cacheable reads; large platforms run both on purpose.
  • Don't lead with a technology name.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "Kafka" or "gRPC, obviously" sounds decisive.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it answers the last question before the first, and two people end up arguing about the consumer while disagreeing about whether anyone waits.
    ↳ Do instead: state the interaction shape first, in the tree's order; the technology falls out.
  • Don't add a protocol a simpler one already covers.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: each new one has a feature the default lacks.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every protocol brings its own auth, retries, rate limits and tracing, and they diverge until an incident or a security review finds the gap.
    ↳ Do instead: keep a default per consumer type, often just REST and one async option, and make every exception argue its weight.
  • Don't forget the browser constraint.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: gRPC looks right for a typed, internal-feeling API that a web app also calls.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a browser can't speak gRPC's HTTP/2 trailers, so the design quietly grows a gRPC-Web proxy or a REST facade.
    ↳ Do instead: settle who the consumer is before choosing; a browser caller rules out gRPC and brokers at the first step.
  • Shelf life: the four questions and the matrix rows are durable. QUERY adoption, the GraphQL-over-HTTP draft and provider streaming choices are what move.

Connections

Path:versioning and deprecationthe choice framework (last in the section)
  • Builds on sync vs async: question one, and the availability arithmetic.
  • Owned elsewhere: REST owns the round-trip arithmetic; choosing a realtime transport owns SSE vs WebSocket.
  • Contrasts with RPC-style APIs: verbs over HTTP, chosen on purpose rather than by accident.
  • Bounded by schemas and contracts: whichever shape wins, the CI gate keeps it from breaking consumers.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: where sync request/response or messaging is chosen per boundary.

notes.title: Schema, Contracts & Compatibility — OpenAPI, Protobuf, the CI Gate
notes.html:
References

📜 OpenAPI Specification 3.2.1 · protobuf.dev: Updating a message type · protobuf.dev: Proto best practices · Buf: Breaking change detection · Pact docs

TL;DR

A contract is real only if something checks it: protobuf through generated code, OpenAPI only when it's generated from the code or validated against traffic. During a rolling deploy old and new versions run together, so a change must work in both directions at once. The control that holds is a CI gate that diffs this commit's schema against the last release.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:schema change in a PRbuf breaking --against last releasenumber reused or type changed? PR failsconsumer contract testspublish stubs per languageconsumers upgrade on their own schedule

Recall

Prompt Answer
Backward vs forward compatible? Backward: new server, old clients. Forward: old code reads the new writer's data.
Deleting a protobuf field safely? reserved its number and its name, so neither is reused.
Which buf category catches a rename? WIRE_JSON or stricter; WIRE ignores names.

The idea

An orders team deletes legacy_status, field 3, and in the same release adds coupon_code as field 3, also a string. Tests pass, the deploy rolls out, and old reporting jobs parse every new order without error, filing SAVE10 as its status. Nothing alerts; the data is just wrong.

A compatibility discipline catches it before merge: a deleted number is reserved forever, and the CI gate compares the new schema with the released one and fails the PR. Rollouts follow an order (add, deploy, write, deploy, rely on it), so every reader in a mixed fleet understands every writer.

The trade: additive-only evolution and a CI gate cost slower, multi-release changes and some schema ceremony; the alternative is breakage that shows up as wrong data, not errors.

How it works

What the gate does with a change, from the cheapest failure to the most expensive.

The diff sees shapes; only contract tests see meaning.

Rule What actually happens
Safe Adding a field with a new number, a method or an endpoint, or an enum value (if readers treat unknown values as unknown). Proto3 parsers keep unknown fields and re-serialise them.
Unsafe on the wire Changing a field's number or type, or reusing a deleted number. Readers misread data silently rather than fail.
Unsafe for code or JSON only Renaming: the binary wire carries numbers, but proto3 JSON, gRPC transcoding and generated code use names.
Tightening Making a field required or narrowing validation rejects requests that used to pass. Protobuf removed required from proto3 for this reason.
The middle A gateway validating requests against OpenAPI, or transcoding JSON to gRPC, enforces the contract it was given, so a stale spec rejects valid traffic.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): OpenAPI 3.2.1 (Sep 2026) for HTTP, protobuf for gRPC and events.
  • Changed in protobuf editions (2024): presence and other behaviour are per-field features rather than proto2/proto3 syntax. The wire is unchanged, so the gate's rules still apply.
  • What won't change: additive change is safe, and meaning changes need a test or a new version.

On the wire

buf breaking 1.75.0 run on 22 Nov 2026 against a released Order (id = 1, total_minor = 2, legacy_status = 3), with id renamed and field 3 reused as an int32. Output trimmed:

buf breaking --against ../old        # buf.yaml: breaking.use: [WIRE_JSON]
# Field "1" on message "Order" changed name from "id" to "order_id".
# Field "1" ... changed option "json_name" from "id" to "orderId".
# Field "3" ... changed type from "string" to "int32".
# exit=100                           ← a failed CI step; with use: [WIRE], only the type change shows

Break it: the scenario from the idea, with schemas built at run time by protobuf 7.36.2 (Python 3.13.14): field 3 deleted and its number reused, same type.

# order_class(): a 9-line helper that builds a message class from a FileDescriptorProto (no protoc)
Old = order_class("v_old", [("id", 1, S), ("total_minor", 2, I), ("legacy_status", 3, S)])
New = order_class("v_new", [("order_id", 1, S), ("total_minor", 2, I), ("coupon_code", 3, S)])
wire = New(order_id="8f2", total_minor=500, coupon_code="SAVE10").SerializeToString()
print(Old.FromString(wire).legacy_status)
# look for: SAVE10, printed with no exception
# naive belief predicts: a parse error, because the schemas disagree

Run on 22 Nov 2026: it printed SAVE10. The same change passed buf breaking under WIRE (exit 0), because a same-type field is wire-compatible; WIRE_JSON and FILE flagged the name change, and deleting the field without reserved failed under both WIRE and FILE.

Measure it

  • See it: buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main', or an OpenAPI diff in CI, exits non-zero on a breaking change; correct is a red PR, not a green deploy.
  • In production: per consumer, gateway schema-validation failures and unknown-enum counts; a spike that clears when a rollout ends is a one-direction change.
  • Bounded by: silent misreads → reserved numbers plus a gate at WIRE_JSON or stricter; semantic breaks → consumer contract tests; unavoidable breaks → a new version (versioning and deprecation).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A contract counts only when something enforces it. Additive changes are safe; removals, type changes and tightening aren't, and the worst misread data silently. Both directions matter, because a rolling deploy mixes versions. The control is a CI gate that diffs against the last release, plus contract tests for meaning.

Q · Mechanism — What counts as a breaking change, precisely? Removing anything a client may use, tightening anything, and changing meaning with the same shape (cents to rupees, a repurposed enum value), which no diff detects. In protobuf, also changing or reusing a field number: in the Break it the reuse passed WIRE and misread silently, so the gate runs at WIRE_JSON or stricter and deleted numbers are reserved.

Q · Trade-off — Generate the spec from the code, or the code from the spec? Code-first can't drift, but the contract becomes an output: you review what you shipped, and internal shapes leak out. Spec-first makes the contract the design artifact, reviewed before code and generating every client, at the cost of a pipeline people route around under deadline. Spec-first for external or cross-team APIs; code-first for one internal consumer. A hand-written spec that neither generates nor is generated is the one wrong answer.

Compare

Contract Enforced by Drifts from code? Breaking-change check When you'd pick it
OpenAPI nothing, unless generated or validated yes, the central risk spec diff in CI HTTP APIs, public and partner
Protobuf generated code no buf breaking gRPC, events, internal
GraphQL schema the server's schema no; it's introspectable schema diff client-shaped reads

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: backward vs forward compatibility
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: "compatible" sounds like one property, and backward is the one everyone tests.
    ↳ Difference: backward means new code accepts old clients and data; forward means old code survives the new writer's data. A rolling deploy needs both at once.
    ↳ Think instead: add, deploy, write, deploy, rely on it: three releases, so every mixed fleet works.
  • "Adding a required field is fine, old clients just won't send it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: adding feels safe, and new clients will send it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: every existing client's request now fails validation, which is the definition of breaking.
    ↳ Think instead: add it optional with a default, migrate clients, and tighten later only if you must.
  • "If it still parses, it's compatible"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the gate is green and every message decodes.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a reused number, a changed unit or a repurposed enum value parses perfectly and is wrong, as the Break it shows.
    ↳ Think instead: shape is checked by the gate, meaning by contract tests or a new field.
  • Don't hand-maintain an OpenAPI file.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: writing YAML is quicker than wiring a generator.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it drifts within weeks, and clients, SDK generators and validating gateways all trust the wrong contract.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: generate it from code and diff it in CI; add spec-first review only for external APIs.
  • Shelf life: the rules are durable; tool versions and buf categories move.
