notes.title: API Authentication — API Keys, OAuth2, JWT, mTLS, HMAC Signing
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9700: OAuth 2.0 Security BCP · 📜 RFC 8725: JWT Best Current Practices · 📜 RFC 7519: JWT · 📜 RFC 9449: DPoP · 📜 RFC 8705: OAuth mTLS · 📜 RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures

TL;DR

Each mechanism answers a different question: an API key says which caller, OAuth says which user let this app act, a JWT is a token format checked without a lookup, mTLS says which workload, and an HMAC signature says this exact request came from you. A bearer token means whoever holds it is you, so the work is in lifetime, audience and binding the token to a key.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:user consentscode + PKCE verifiershort access token + refresh tokenAuthorization: Bearergateway checks signature, pinned alg, exp, iss, audforwards identity over mTLSservice checks scope

Recall

Prompt Answer
The JWT check that stops alg: none forgery? Pin the accepted algorithms; never trust the token's own alg (RFC 8725 §3.1).
Grants RFC 9700 retires? Implicit: SHOULD NOT. Resource-owner password: MUST NOT.
Why can't you revoke a stateless JWT early? Nothing is looked up; it lives until exp, unless you add introspection or a denylist.

The idea

A partner leaks an access token in a support ticket. It's a JWT valid for 24 hours, every service validates it locally, and nothing can stop it until it expires. Worse, the same issuer mints tokens for the billing and the search service, and search's token works on billing because billing never checks aud.

Current practice changes each part. Access tokens live minutes and a safer-held refresh token renews them, so revoking it ends access within one lifetime. Every validator checks aud, a MUST when one issuer serves several audiences (RFC 8725 §3.9). And RFC 9700 says tokens SHOULD be sender-constrained, with DPoP (RFC 9449) or mTLS (RFC 8705), so a leaked token is useless without the client's key.

The trade: stateless validation is fast and needs no shared store, and you pay with revocation that waits for expiry unless you add a lookup back.

How it works

Authorization code with PKCE, then one validation at the gateway; consent happens earlier, in the browser.

One validator; services trust mTLS for the workload and propagated claims for the user.

Rule What actually happens
PKCE for every client RFC 9700 applies it to web apps too, with S256; it also gives CSRF protection on the redirect.
Exact redirect matching The auth server compares redirect URIs as exact strings; open redirectors leak codes and tokens.
Lifetime is the exposure window A leaked 15-minute token works up to 15 minutes. Instant revocation means introspection per request, giving up statelessness.
Never in the URL RFC 6750 §2.3 says a query-string token SHOULD NOT be used: access logs, proxy logs and history keep it.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026). OAuth 2.0 dates from 2012; RFC 9700 (Jan 2025) is the current security baseline. OAuth 2.1 is still an Internet-Draft (draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-17).
  • Changed in RFC 9700: implicit grant SHOULD NOT be used, password grant MUST NOT, PKCE is expected everywhere, and public clients' refresh tokens MUST be sender-constrained or rotated.
  • What's next: DPoP replacing plain bearer tokens on high-value APIs. What won't change: the five questions.

On the wire

Break it: a validator that lets the token pick its own algorithm. A forged token with alg: none and an empty signature (base64 and HMAC helpers trimmed):

def naive(tok):                                    # trusts the token's own "alg"
    h, p, s = tok.split("."); alg = unb64(h)["alg"]
    if alg == "none": return unb64(p)              # "no signature needed"
    return unb64(p) if valid_hs256(h, p, s) else "rejected"
def pinned(tok):                                   # RFC 8725 §3.1: the caller picks the algorithm
    return "rejected" if unb64(tok.split(".")[0])["alg"] != "HS256" else naive(tok)
forged = f'{b64({"alg": "none"})}.{b64({"sub": "admin", "aud": "billing"})}.'
print("naive: ", naive(forged)); print("pinned:", pinned(forged))
# look for: naive returns the forged claims, pinned rejects them
# naive belief predicts: both reject, because "the token isn't signed"

Run on Python 3.15, standard library only: naive: {'sub': 'admin', 'aud': 'billing'}, pinned: rejected. The attacker chose to skip the signature check.

Measure it

  • See it: decode a token (cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d) and check alg, exp, aud; send one with a wrong aud and expect 401.
  • In production: per consumer, 401 and 403 rates by reason (expired, bad audience, bad signature) and refresh failures. A bad-audience spike is a misconfigured caller or a probe.
  • Bounded by: a leaked token → short lifetime plus refresh revocation, then sender-constraining (DPoP or mTLS) so the token alone is useless.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Five mechanisms for five questions. API keys identify a caller. OAuth delegates a user's consent to an app, with scopes. JWT is the token format that validates without a lookup, which is why it's fast and why revocation waits for expiry. mTLS authenticates the workload at the transport, which a mesh makes cheap. HMAC signs a request so a receiver knows it's unaltered. Production layers them: mTLS between services plus a short-lived user token.

Q · Mechanism — What must a JWT validator actually check? The signature, against a key from your configuration or a JWKS you trust, never a URL in the token. The algorithm, from your allow-list (the Break it). exp and nbf with small skew. iss, refusing other issuers. aud, so a token minted for another service fails despite a valid signature. Then scopes, in the owning service. Doing it once at the gateway stops services diverging.

Q · Trade-off — Bearer tokens or mTLS between services? Bearer tokens are flexible: one mechanism for browsers, partners and services, rotated by a refresh. Their weakness is the name: a token in a log is a credential. mTLS binds identity to a key that never travels and is nearly free in a mesh, but it names the workload, not the user, and needs certificate rotation you actually operate (mTLS). The answer at scale is both, and RFC 8705's certificate-bound tokens join them.

Compare

Answers Revocation Leak impact When you'd pick it
API key which caller? delete the key full access until rotated low-risk server-to-server
OAuth + JWT did the user let this app act? waits for exp until expiry user delegation, public APIs
mTLS which workload? revoke or expire the cert none: the key never travels service to service
HMAC signature is this request yours, unaltered? rotate the secret until rotated webhooks (webhooks)

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Registered JWT claims 7 iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti spec: RFC 7519 §4.1
PKCE challenge method S256 the only one that hides the verifier spec: RFC 9700 §2.1.1

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: authentication vs authorisation
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both live in the same header and the same middleware.
    ↳ Difference: authentication proves who is calling (signature, iss, aud); authorisation decides whether they may do this (scopes, resource ownership).
    ↳ Think instead: the gateway authenticates once; the owning service authorises against its own data.
  • "JWTs are more secure than session cookies"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they're signed and newer.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: they're differently shaped. A session id is revocable because it's looked up; a JWT trades that away for local validation.
    ↳ Think instead: a JWT checked against a store on every request is a session with extra parsing.
  • Don't rely on mTLS alone for user-facing authorisation.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's strong, mutual and already on in the mesh.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it tells you the checkout service is calling, not which user is behind the request, so any user's request passes.
    ↳ Do instead: propagate a user token or verified claims alongside the mTLS identity.
  • Don't hand-roll request signing.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: an HMAC over the body is five lines.
    ↳ What goes wrong: bespoke schemes forget the timestamp, sign a re-serialised body, or compare with == instead of a constant-time check.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, or your provider's verified library.
  • Shelf life: OAuth 2.1's final form and DPoP adoption will move.

Connections

Path:schemas and contractsAPI authenticationversioning and deprecation
  • Owned elsewhere: mTLS owns the handshake; webhooks owns the HMAC + timestamp window.
  • Used by API gateway: where validation runs once.
  • Used by AI-stack protocols: bearer tokens on a remote MCP endpoint.
  • Bounded by rate limiting: per-key limits cap a leaked key's damage.

notes.title: API Versioning and Deprecation — Changing a Public Contract Without Breaking Clients
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9745: The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field · 📜 RFC 8594: The Sunset HTTP Header Field · 📜 RFC 8288: Web Linking

TL;DR

The cheapest version is the one you never ship: additive change keeps one contract alive for years. When a break is unavoidable, run both, mark the old one in every response with Deprecation and Sunset, and retire on per-consumer telemetry, not on a calendar: you can announce a sunset without it, but you can't finish one.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:v2 + migration guidev1 responses carry Deprecation, Sunset, Link rel="deprecation"count distinct consumers on v1outreach by namescheduled brown-outszero consumersretire v1

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two headers, and their formats? Deprecation: @<epoch> (RFC 9745), Sunset: <HTTP-date> (RFC 8594).
Their ordering rule? Sunset MUST NOT be earlier than Deprecation (RFC 9745 §4).
The metric that gates retirement? Distinct consumers still calling v1, not v1's share of traffic.

The idea

You ship v2 and post a changelog entry: "v1 ends in six months". On the day, v1 still carries a little traffic, and nobody can say whether it is a health check or a partner's payroll run. So you extend, and extend again, and three years later four versions are live and none is retirable.

What changes it is making the deprecation machine-readable and attributable. Every v1 response says when it was deprecated and when it stops, with a link to the guide, so SDKs can warn, partners' monitoring can alert and your gateway can count. Every v1 call is attributed to a consumer, so the question becomes "which 40 clients are left?". Then you contact them by name and run a scheduled brown-out so the last callers find their dependency while someone is watching.

The trade: a retirement you can finish, paid for with two code paths for the whole window and the telemetry to attribute every call.

How it works

A version's lifecycle. Deprecation changes nothing about behaviour (RFC 9745 §5); only the sunset does.

Rule What actually happens
What counts as breaking Owned by schemas and contracts: removal, renaming, new required input. Avoiding those removes most reasons for a v2.
Where the version lives URL path versus header is decided in REST API design; version the whole surface, never per endpoint.
The headers Deprecation is a Structured Field date (@ + epoch seconds), past or future. Sunset is an HTTP-date, and clients SHOULD treat it as a hint (RFC 8594 §3).
Attribution Per-consumer keys, the same identity rate limiting uses (rate limiting). No key, no retirement.
The middle The gateway stamps the headers, counts callers per version, and runs the brown-out; SDKs log a warning when they see Deprecation.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): Sunset since RFC 8594 (May 2019, Informational); Deprecation became RFC 9745 (Standards Track) in March 2025.
  • Changed in RFC 9745: the value is a Structured Field date (@1688169599), not an HTTP-date like Sunset; a deprecation link relation points at the guide.
  • What's next: gateways and OpenAPI tooling emitting both headers by default. What won't change: retirement is gated on the last consumer.

On the wire

Captured on 22 Nov 2026 from an http.server handler on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15, curl 8.7.1), a v1 read deprecated from 1 Jan 2027:

GET /v1/orders/8f2
HTTP/1.0 200 OK                                    # behaviour unchanged: deprecation is a signal
Deprecation: @1798761600                           # 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z, Structured Field date
Sunset: Mon, 01 Nov 2027 00:00:00 GMT              # HTTP-date, and not earlier than Deprecation
Link: <https://api.example.com/docs/v2-migration>; rel="deprecation"; type="text/html"
{"id": "8f2"}

Measure it

  • See it: curl -i on any v1 route shows both headers and the Link; a route without them is a deprecation nobody's code will notice.
  • In production: distinct consumer ids calling v1 per week, per endpoint, and their last-seen date; brown-out error counts by consumer. A share-of-traffic chart near zero hides the 40 callers that gate retirement.
  • Bounded by: a cut-off that breaks a silent consumer → per-consumer attribution, direct outreach, and brown-outs of growing length (an hour, then a day) before the sunset.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The best versioning strategy is not shipping a new version: additive change, tolerant readers and an unknown enum value avoid most breaks. When one is unavoidable, run both versions, mark every old response with Deprecation, Sunset and a link to the guide, and drive retirement from per-consumer telemetry. Brown-out before you black-out, so the last callers find out while you're watching.

Q · Mechanism — How do you retire a version without breaking people? In order: publish v2 and the migration guide together, because a deprecation with nowhere to go is a threat. Stamp every v1 response with the headers so the signal reaches code, not only changelog readers. Attribute every v1 call to a consumer. Contact the remaining ones by name, repeatedly. Then brown out on a schedule: errors for an hour, then a day. The skipped step is attribution, and it's the one the rest depends on: without it, you can't tell a probe from a bank.

Q · Trade-off — How long do you support the old version? Set it by consumer class, not one number: internal callers you can page move quickly; first-party mobile apps take as long as old installs stay in use, because you can't force an upgrade; partners need what their contracts say. The cost side gets under-weighted: two code paths, every fix made twice, and a data model that must satisfy both, which constrains the design v2 was for. Publish the window as policy before the first deprecation, and spend the effort on not needing it.

Compare

Channel Reaches Misses When you'd pick it
Changelog or blog post people who read changelogs the code that calls you always, but never alone
Deprecation + Sunset headers SDKs, monitoring, your gateway's counts clients that ignore headers every deprecated response
Direct outreach by consumer id the owner of each remaining caller consumers you can't attribute the last few dozen callers
Scheduled brown-out whoever still depends on v1, while you watch nothing that calls during the window before any hard cut-off

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Deprecation value @ + epoch seconds a Structured Field Date spec: RFC 9745 §2, RFC 9651 §3.3.7
Sunset value HTTP-date a hint, not a guarantee spec: RFC 8594 §3
Ordering Sunset ≥ Deprecation otherwise ask the provider spec: RFC 9745 §4

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: deprecated vs sunset
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "the old version is going away", often announced together.
    ↳ Difference: deprecated means "still works, stop building on it", and behaviour is unchanged; sunset is the time it stops responding.
    ↳ Think instead: Deprecation starts the clock, Sunset ends it, and the gap is the migration window.
  • "Traffic on v1 is at 0.3%, so we're nearly done"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: share of traffic is the chart every dashboard already has.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: retirement is gated on the last consumer, not the volume; 0.3% from 40 consumers is further from done than 4% from one known caller.
    ↳ Think instead: count distinct consumers, and know each one by name.
  • Don't ship v2 as a rewrite.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: if you're breaking anyway, fix everything at once.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the bigger the delta, the fewer consumers migrate and the longer both versions run.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler path: break only what must break, keep the rest identical, and make the guide a short diff.
  • Don't hard-cut without a brown-out.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the date was announced months ago, so everyone has been warned.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the silent consumer finds out at 3 a.m. on cut-off day, as an incident on both sides.
    ↳ Do instead: scheduled error windows while your team is watching turn a future incident into a controlled discovery.
  • Shelf life: the headers and the telemetry-first retirement are durable. Tooling that emits them by default is what's still spreading.

Connections

Path:API authenticationversioning and deprecationthe choice framework
  • Builds on schemas and contracts: what counts as breaking, and the CI gate that catches it.
  • Owned elsewhere: REST API design owns URL vs header versioning.
  • Composes with rate limiting: the same per-consumer identity attributes every call.
  • Decided in service communication patterns: API versioning and contract evolution between services.
